senses.definition: A randomized controlled experiment in which users are randomly split between two versions (A and B) of a product, page or model to measure which performs better on a chosen metric.
To compare two versions by running such an experiment.

core.definition: A randomized experiment that splits users between two versions, A and B, to measure which performs better on a chosen metric.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters 'A' and 'B' with the stronger beat on B; the slash is not pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in tech it signals a data-driven decision.
nuance.usage_note: American product, marketing and data teams say this constantly: 'let's A/B test it,' 'the A/B test is still running.' It is used as both a noun and a verb, and 'A/B testing' names the practice. For an AI model, teams often A/B test a new model against the current one on live traffic.

distinctions.note: A multivariate test varies several elements at once to measure their combinations; an A/B test compares two versions.
An A/A test shows the same version to both groups to check that the experiment setup itself is unbiased.
A bandit shifts traffic toward the better variant while the test runs; a classic A/B test keeps a fixed split until it ends.

examples.everyday: My sister's company ran an A/B test on two signup buttons, and the green one won.
examples.professional: Before we roll out the new ranking model, let's A/B test it against production for two weeks with a pre-registered primary metric.
examples.analytical: An A/B test estimates the average treatment effect only for the population and period sampled, so novelty effects can mislead a short test.

nuance.analogy: An A/B test is a clinical trial for a product: half the users get the new pill, half get the old one, and chance decides who is who.
nuance.etymology: From the conventional names A (control) and B (variant).
common_mistakes: Stopping the test as soon as the result looks significant ('peeking'), which inflates false positives.
Writing 'AB test' or 'A-B test'; the standard spelling is A/B test.

a/b-test.etymology: From the labels *A* and *B* for the two variants compared.

core.definition: In the Book of Kings, the name of a king of Judah who reigned briefly after Rehoboam, also called Abijah in Chronicles.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BY, and the last syllable rhymes with 'jam'. Keep the first vowel reduced and do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: This is a proper name used for a specific biblical king, so it is used in Bible study, sermons, or historical discussion of Judah. In the American Bible study context, people often note the name difference between Kings and Chronicles.

distinctions.note: Abijah is the name used in Chronicles for the same king, while Abijam is the form used in the Book of Kings. The Hebrew forms differ only slightly.

examples.everyday: Abijam is a name I only ever see in Kings, so I looked up that he is the same person as Abijah.
examples.professional: When teaching the divided monarchy, I note that Abijam in Kings and Abijah in Chronicles refer to the same king of Judah.
examples.analytical: The variant spelling Abijam in 1 Kings 15 and Abijah in 2 Chronicles 13 reflects differing textual or historiographical traditions about the same reign.

nuance.etymology: A variant form of Abijah from Hebrew, usually taken to mean 'my father is Yah'.
common_mistakes: Treating Abijam and Abijah as two different kings.
Stressing the final syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Abijam (Hebrew Abiyyam) is the name given to the king of Judah in 1 Kings 15:1-8, who reigned for about three years after Rehoboam. The same king is called Abijah in 2 Chronicles 13. The two forms are a case of variant names in the Hebrew Bible, and the story of his wars with Jeroboam appears in both books, though with different emphases.

senses.definition: The act of washing something.
The act of washing or cleansing the body, or some part of it, as a religious rite.
Washing oneself; bathing, cleaning oneself up.
The rinsing of the priest's hand and the sacred vessel following the Communion with, depending on rite, water or a mix of it and wine, which may then be drunk by the priest.
Wudu, ritual washing of the limbs and head performed immediately before prayer or holding the Quran.
The liquid used in the cleansing or ablution.
The ritual consumption by the deacon or priest of leftover sacred wine of host after the Communion.
Originally, the purifying of oils and other substances by emulsification with hot water; now more generally, a thorough cleansing of a precipitate or other non-dissolved substance.

core.definition: A ritual washing of the body or a part of it, performed as a religious act before worship or prayer.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BLOO, the second syllable, and the last syllable is a light 'shun.' Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or add a strong vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to reverent. It describes a religious practice, and in humorous speech it can refer to morning grooming.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ablution mostly in religious studies, literature, or describing practices like wudu before Muslim prayer. In casual speech, people say 'wash up' or 'get ready.' Joking about your 'morning ablutions' is a playful way to talk about washing your face and brushing your teeth.

distinctions.note: Purification refers to any cleansing of the spirit or body, ritual or not. Ablution specifically means the physical washing that is part of a ritual.
A bath is an ordinary act of cleaning yourself. An ablution is a ritual act with religious meaning.

examples.everyday: I'm running late, so I'll skip my morning ablutions and just splash some water on my face.
examples.professional: The hotel's prayer room has a small space for ablutions, so guests can wash before they pray.
examples.analytical: In the ritual, the ablutions mark a transition from the profane world to the sacred, making the body ready for worship.

nuance.analogy: Like rinsing your hands and face before walking into a sacred room, as a sign of respect.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ablutio, 'a washing away', from abluere, 'to wash off', from ab- plus lavere, 'to wash'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (AB-lution) instead of BLOO.
Using ablution for everyday dish washing or showering in ordinary speech.
Using the singular for a general plural activity; morning ablutions is the common joking form.

ablution.etymology: From Middle English *ablucioun* (“cleansing of impurities”), from Old French *ablution*, and its source, Late Latin *ablūtiō* (“a washing away”), from *abluō* (“wash away”), from *ab* + *lavō*.

senses.definition: The act of abolishing; an annulling; abrogation.
senses.example: the abolition of debts; the abolition of laws; the abolition of slavery; the abolition of police; the abolition of taxes

senses.definition: The state of being abolished.
The ending of the slave trade or of slavery.

core.definition: The formal ending of a law, institution, or practice, especially slavery. Also the act of officially canceling something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, LISH, and the final -tion is pronounced like 'shun'. Don't pronounce the middle 'o' as a clear 'oh'; it reduces to a short 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in historical and legal contexts, but strongly charged when it refers to slavery, where it is associated with moral triumph. Outside that context it can sound stiff.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech, 'abolition' most often refers to ending slavery, as in the abolition movement. In a general sense, Americans are more likely to say 'elimination', 'ending', or 'repeal' for laws and practices. Using 'abolition' for a company policy or small rule may sound overly dramatic or formal.

distinctions.note: Elimination is the everyday word for removing something; abolition implies formally ending a legal institution or long-standing practice.
Repeal means canceling a specific law; abolition means ending the whole institution or practice that law supported.

collocations: the abolition of the death penalty

examples.everyday: My grandmother still talks about the abolition of the old school dress code, and she was thrilled when it finally happened.
examples.professional: Our policy team is pushing for the abolition of the manual approval step, since it slows every deployment by two days.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the abolition of slavery was not a single event but a long political struggle involving law, religion, and economic change.

nuance.analogy: Abolition is like tearing down a building entirely, rather than just repairing one room.
nuance.etymology: From Latin abolere, meaning 'to destroy' or 'do away with', via French abolition.
common_mistakes: Using 'abolition' for minor rules; in everyday English, 'elimination' or 'removal' is more natural.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying ab-uh-LEE-shun instead of ab-uh-LISH-un.

senses.definition: In an abominable manner; very odiously; detestably.

core.definition: In a very bad, unpleasant, or disgusting way. Used to intensify negative qualities.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on BAH, the second syllable. The final '-ly' is pronounced 'lee', and the middle syllables are reduced to weak 'uh' vowels.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It intensifies an unpleasant quality, often with a sense of exaggeration in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'abominably' mostly in writing or in formal speech, and occasionally in casual complaints. In everyday talk, 'really bad' or 'awfully' is more natural. Using 'abominably' with a positive adjective is not natural.

distinctions.note: Terribly is a common everyday intensifier; abominably is stronger and more formal, suggesting disgust.
Awfully is casual and common in speech; abominably sounds more formal and literary.

examples.everyday: The waiter was abominably rude, and he didn't even apologize when our soup came out cold.
examples.professional: Our test coverage was abominably low, so the release was delayed until the team added more automated checks.
examples.analytical: The committee's report treated the evidence abominably, ignoring every study that contradicted its conclusion.

nuance.analogy: If something is abominable, then doing it abominably means doing it so badly that people are disgusted.
nuance.etymology: Derived from abominable, from Latin abominari, 'to deprecate as an ill omen'.
common_mistakes: Using 'abominably' with positive words, such as 'abominably good'.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'ab-uh-MIN-uh-blee'; the stress stays on the second syllable.

senses.definition: Producing abrasion; rough enough to wear away the outer surface.
Being rough and coarse in manner or disposition; overly aggressive and causing irritation.
senses.example: An abrasive person can grate on one's sensibilities.

senses.definition: A hard inorganic substance or material consisting in powder or granule form such as sandpaper, pumice, or emery, used for cleaning, smoothing, or polishing.
Rock fragments, sand grains, mineral particles, used by water, wind, and ice to abrade a land surface.

core.definition: Harsh and rough in manner, likely to irritate or annoy people; also rough enough to wear away a surface.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BRAY. The final -sive is pronounced 'siv', with a short i, not 'seev'.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing people or tone, as in 'an abrasive personality.' Neutral or technical when describing materials like abrasive cleaners.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'abrasive' to describe a coworker or a manager who is blunt and harsh, or a comment that sounds rude. It is a polite but clear criticism, so use it carefully about people. The noun form for materials, such as 'abrasives', is mostly used in manufacturing or hardware stores.

distinctions.note: Harsh is broader and can describe weather, sounds, or treatment; abrasive focuses on a rough, irritating way of dealing with people.
Blunt means direct and honest in speech; abrasive means the directness feels unpleasant or irritating to others.

examples.everyday: My brother is a good guy, but his jokes can be pretty abrasive when he's stressed.
examples.professional: Feedback in the code review was accurate, but the tone was too abrasive, so people stopped commenting.
examples.analytical: The author argues that abrasive rhetoric can win attention in public debate while eroding the trust needed for lasting cooperation.

nuance.analogy: Like a coarse sponge that scrubs your skin raw when you wanted a gentle wash.
nuance.etymology: From Latin abrasus, the past participle of abradere, meaning to scrape off.
common_mistakes: Using abrasive as a verb, when the verb is abrade.
Calling a person an abrasive in a formal sentence, where it is better to say 'abrasive person' or 'has an abrasive manner'.

senses.definition: Increase by natural growth, especially the gradual increase of organic bodies by the internal addition of matter; organic growth; also, the amount of such growth.
(Gradual) increase by an external addition of matter; an instance of this.
senses.example: A mineral augments not by growth, but by accretion.

senses.definition: Followed by of: external addition of matter to a thing which causes it to grow, especially in amount or size.
The process of separate particles aggregating or coalescing together; concretion; a thing formed in this manner.
senses.example: The accretion of particles forms a solid mass.

senses.definition: The formation of planets, stars, and other celestial bodies by the aggregating of matter drawn together by gravity; also, the growth of a celestial body through this process.
Something gradually added to or growing on a thing externally.
senses.example: accretion of ice

senses.definition: A substance which has built up on the surface of an object, rather than become embedded in it.
senses.example: Accretions of dirt on clothing are often left in place by conservators because they can provide additional details about the artefact’s importance or history.

senses.definition: The process by which material is added to a geological feature; specifically, to a tectonic plate at a subduction zone.

Increase in property by the addition of other property to it (for example, gain of land by alluvion (“the deposition of sediment by a river or sea”) or dereliction (“recession of water from the usual watermark”), or entitlement to the products of the property such as interest on money); or by the property owner acquiring another person’s ownership rights; accession; an instance of this.
Increase of an inheritance to an heir or legatee due to the share of a co-heir or co-legatee being added to it, because the latter person is legally unable to inherit the share.

core.definition: The gradual buildup of material over time, either from natural growth or from matter added from outside.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KREE. The -tion ending is pronounced 'shun', and the first syllable is a reduced 'uh'. Do not pronounce the t as a separate sound before the sh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is descriptive, though in finance an accretion of value is positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in science (planets, glaciers, coral reefs), finance (accretion of a bond's discount), and academic writing. In everyday talk, say buildup. The word sounds formal, so in a casual conversation it may sound like jargon.

distinctions.note: Buildup is everyday and general; accretion is technical and implies material added in layers, often through a gradual natural process.
Accrual is a bookkeeping term for amounts recorded as they accumulate; accretion is about physical or natural growth, though finance also uses it for bond discounts.

examples.everyday: That old kettle has years of mineral accretion inside, so it takes forever to boil.
examples.professional: The accretion of technical debt in our codebase is slowing every release, so we need a cleanup sprint.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether the nation's identity formed through sudden revolution or through slow accretion of custom and law.

nuance.analogy: Accretion is like a snowball rolling downhill, collecting more snow as it goes.
nuance.etymology: From Latin accretio, from accrescere 'to grow to', from ad- 'to' and crescere 'to grow'.
common_mistakes: Using accretion for sudden additions; it implies slow, cumulative growth.
Pronouncing it with stress on the first syllable, as in AK-ree-shun, instead of uh-KREE-shun.

senses.definition: To bring forward or offer, as an argument, passage, or consideration which bears on a statement or case.
To produce as proof.
senses.example: At this juncture, he sought to establish the awareness of the activity; to that end, he then adduced the receipts from the transactions of June 30th.

core.definition: To present evidence, a reason, or an example to support an argument or claim.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable and pronounce the final vowel like the 'oo' in 'goose', so it rhymes with 'juice'. Learners often say 'uh-DYOOS' with an extra y sound, which sounds British and unnatural in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes the careful presentation of support for a position, but it can sound stiff in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use adduce in academic papers, legal argument, philosophy, and formal debate, typically with evidence or reasons as the object. In everyday talk, people say 'give' or 'cite' instead. Using adduce in a casual conversation can sound overly formal or pretentious.

distinctions.note: Cite usually refers to naming a specific source or authority, while adduce refers to presenting any kind of evidence or reasoning to support a claim.
Allege means to claim without proof, while adduce means to offer actual support for a claim.

examples.everyday: When my roommate said the store was closed, I asked her to adduce some proof, like a sign or a website.
examples.professional: Before we change the pricing model, we need to adduce data showing that the current one is hurting retention.
examples.analytical: The philosopher adduces several thought experiments to show that intuition alone cannot justify the moral claim.

nuance.analogy: To adduce evidence is like placing bricks on the table one by one to show the wall you plan to build.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adducere, 'to lead or bring to,' from ad-, 'to,' and ducere, 'to lead.'
common_mistakes: Confusing adduce with deduce, which means to reach a conclusion by reasoning.
Pronouncing it 'uh-DYOOS' with a y sound, which is less common in American English.

adduce.etymology: From Middle English *adducen*, from Latin *addūcō*, *adductus* (“to lead or bring to”), from *ad-* + *dūcō* (“to lead”).

senses.definition: Expressing opposition or difference.
Expressing adverse effect.
(dated, rare) Something, particularly a clause or conjunction, which is adversative.
senses.label: dated, rare

core.definition: Expressing contrast or opposition between two ideas, as with the words but, however or yet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on vur, the second syllable, and the final tive is a reduced syllable. Learners often stress the first syllable or pronounce the r too weakly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a grammatical or rhetorical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in grammar, linguistics, rhetoric and academic writing. In conversation, you would just say 'but' or 'however'. Teachers and writers might call a clause adversative, and the noun form is used in the same way. It is not a common everyday word.

distinctions.note: Adversative describes a logical or grammatical relation of contrast, while adversarial describes people or systems that are opposed to each other.
Contrastive is a broader term for showing difference, while adversative specifically signals opposition or a counter-point.

examples.everyday: You'd just say but in conversation, though grammarians call it an adversative conjunction.
examples.professional: In the report, the word however is adversative, signaling that the second finding complicates the first.
examples.analytical: The adversative relation in faith is strong, yet doubt persists marks a tension rather than a simple contradiction.

nuance.analogy: Like a sign that turns the road sharply, the word tells you the direction of the thought is about to change.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin adversativus, opposing, from Latin adversari, to oppose.
common_mistakes: Confusing adversative with adverse or adversarial, which have different meanings.
Using adversative as a common everyday word; say but or however instead in speech.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'AD-ver-SAY-tiv'.

senses.definition: The act of affecting or acting upon.

The state of being affected, especially: a change in, or alteration of, the emotional state of a person or other animal, caused by a subjective affect (a subjective feeling or emotion), which arises in response to a stimulus which may result from either thought or perception.
An attribute; a quality or property; a condition.
An emotion; a feeling or natural impulse acting upon and swaying the mind.
A feeling of love or strong attachment; a feeling of enjoyable and comforting fondness.
senses.example: I have a lot of affection for my little sister.

senses.definition: (rare) To feel affection for.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A warm feeling of fondness or love toward a person, pet or thing, often shown through affectionate behavior.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FEK, the second syllable. The ending '-tion' is pronounced 'shun,' and the first syllable is a reduced 'uh.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests warmth, kindness and closeness, though it can sound slightly formal in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'affection' for loving feelings toward family, friends or pets, and they often say 'show affection' or 'with affection' in letters. In casual conversation people more often say 'love,' 'fondness' or 'care for.' The word can also appear in a sign-off, as in 'With affection, Mom.'

distinctions.note: 'Love' is broader and stronger, and it is the common everyday word, while 'affection' usually suggests a gentler, warm fondness.
'Affectation' means an unnatural way of behaving to impress others, so it is very different from genuine affection.

examples.everyday: My dog shows so much affection when I come home that it makes my whole day.
examples.professional: I wanted to express my affection for the team with a short thank-you note after the launch.
examples.analytical: Aristotle distinguishes friendship based on affection from friendship based on usefulness or pleasure.

nuance.analogy: Affection is like a warm lamp in a room: it is steady and gentle, and it makes a space feel welcoming.
nuance.etymology: From Latin affectio, a disposition or state of mind, from afficere, to act upon, from ad- plus facere, to make.
common_mistakes: Using 'affection' for an illness or disease; in medical language it can mean a condition, but in everyday English it means fondness.
Confusing 'affection' with 'affectation,' which describes fake behavior.

affection.etymology: From Middle English *affection*, *affeccion*, *affeccioun*, from Old French *affection*, from Latin *affectiōnem*, from *affectiō*; equivalent to *affect* + *ion*.

senses.definition: A bound morpheme added to a word’s stem, such as a prefix or suffix.
The complex number a+bi associated with the point in the Gauss plane with coordinates (a,b).
Any small feature, as a figure, a flower, or the like, added for ornament to a vessel or other utensil, to an architectural feature.
(rare, uncommon) That which is affixed; an appendage.
senses.label: rare, uncommon

senses.definition: To attach.
senses.example: to affix a stigma to a person

senses.definition: To subjoin, annex, or add at the close or end; to append to.
senses.example: to affix a syllable to a word

senses.definition: To fix or fasten figuratively.
senses.example: eyes affixed upon the ground

core.definition: In linguistics, a bound morpheme, such as a prefix or suffix, attached to a word stem to change its meaning or grammatical form.

pronunciation.tip: Noun stress falls on the first syllable: AF-iks. As a verb, the word is stressed on the second syllable: uh-FIX. Do not pronounce the final 'x' as 'ks' with a separate 'ex' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in grammar and linguistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use affix mainly in linguistics, grammar, language teaching, and spelling instruction. In everyday talk, people say 'prefix' or 'suffix' if they mean a specific kind. The noun and verb are pronounced differently, so you need to change the stress when you switch from one to the other.

distinctions.note: A prefix is one type of affix that comes before the stem, as in 'unhappy'.
A suffix is one type of affix that comes after the stem, as in 'happiness'.

examples.everyday: My English teacher said the affix un- makes a word mean not, like unhappy.
examples.professional: The tokenizer treats each common affix as a separate token so that the model can recognize related word forms.
examples.analytical: In agglutinative languages, a single stem may take several affixes, each adding one grammatical meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like a sticker added to a box: it attaches to the main thing and changes what it says.
nuance.etymology: From Latin affixus, the past participle of affigere, 'to fasten to'.
common_mistakes: Using the noun pronunciation AF-iks for the verb; the verb is uh-FIX.
Using affix when prefix or suffix is more precise for a specific position.

senses.definition: Offering unlimited food to a diner at a restaurant for a fixed price for as long as the diner continues to eat.
Offering unlimited service for a fixed price per time period.
An all-you-can-eat restaurant.

core.definition: Offering unlimited food for one fixed price, so customers can keep eating as much as they want.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on EAT. In fast speech 'you can' often blurs to 'yoo-kin', so it sounds like 'awl yoo-kin-EET'.

nuance.connotation: Positive for value, but it can suggest overeating or low quality, depending on the restaurant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'all-you-can-eat buffet' or 'AYCE' on signs for restaurants that offer unlimited food at a fixed price, often for lunch or dinner. It is casual and common in everyday talk. A natural reply is 'Sounds good, what time should we go?'

distinctions.note: A buffet is a spread that you serve yourself, but it is not always unlimited, while 'all-you-can-eat' emphasizes unlimited food for one price.
A prix fixe meal is a fixed set menu at a fixed price with limited choices, while all-you-can-eat offers unlimited quantity with many options.

examples.everyday: Let's go to that all-you-can-eat sushi place on Friday.
examples.professional: We booked an all-you-can-eat lunch for the offsite, so the food budget is fixed.
examples.analytical: All-you-can-eat pricing makes each extra plate cost the diner nothing, which is why restaurants use it to attract large appetites.

nuance.analogy: Like an open tab at a bar, but for food.
nuance.etymology: A compound formed in English from the plain words 'all you can eat', describing the terms of the deal.
common_mistakes: Saying 'all you can eats' with a plural; the phrase is singular as an adjective or noun.
Using 'all-you-can-eat' as a verb; say 'eat as much as you want' instead.

conversation.text: They have all-you-can-eat crab legs on Thursday nights.
Don't eat lunch before going to an all-you-can-eat place.
The all-you-can-eat sushi deal was twenty-nine dollars.

core.definition: An Old Testament name borne by several men, most notably a king of Judah who fought Israel and was later killed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ZY, the second half of the middle syllable. The final -ah is a weak schwa, so it sounds like 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a proper name with no positive or negative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Amaziah is a name used in Bible reading, sermons and church classes. Americans do not use it in everyday conversation, and they mostly meet it in 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles and the book of Amos.

distinctions.note: Amasa was a commander under Absalom; Amaziah was a king of Judah, and the names are easy to confuse.

examples.everyday: Our pastor mentioned Amaziah, the king who picked a fight with Israel and lost his kingdom's wealth.
examples.professional: In my sermon prep I compare Amaziah's overconfidence with the story of the king who refused the prophet's warning.
examples.analytical: The Chronicler presents Amaziah's defeat as a consequence of his refusal to heed a prophet's warning after his victory over Edom, as recorded in 2 Chronicles 25:14-16.

nuance.etymology: Hebrew 'Amatsyahu', commonly rendered 'Yahweh is strong'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (AM-uh-zy-uh)
Confusing Amaziah with Amasa or Amos
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew 'Amatsyahu', commonly rendered 'Yahweh is strong'. 2 Kings 14:1-20 describes Amaziah's reign as king of Judah, his war with Jehoash of Israel and his defeat at Beth-shemesh. 2 Kings 14:19 reports that conspirators killed him at Lachish. Amos 7:10-17 describes Amaziah the priest of Bethel ordering the prophet Amos to leave the sanctuary.

senses.definition: A drink made of espresso coffee diluted with hot water.
A cocktail made with Campari, sweet vermouth, and club soda.

core.definition: A coffee drink made by diluting espresso with hot water, giving a milder, longer cup than straight espresso.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KAH, the third-from-last syllable, not on MAIR as in America. The first and second syllables are weak, so say them quickly, and keep the r in mair.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is an ordinary coffee-shop order with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans order this at cafés with 'Can I get an Americano?' and specify 'iced' or 'with oat milk' if they want something different. A drip coffee is a different drink, so if you want regular brewed coffee, say 'coffee' or 'drip coffee'. In a bar, the word can refer to a Campari cocktail, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Drip coffee is brewed by pouring hot water through ground beans, while an Americano is espresso shots with added hot water.
A long black is an Australian and New Zealand drink made by pouring espresso over hot water, so the order is reversed; Americans would not use this term.

examples.everyday: Can I get a large Americano with a little room, please?
examples.professional: I grabbed an Americano from the cafe downstairs before the sprint review.
examples.analytical: An Americano dilutes espresso's concentration, so its flavor is milder and more like drip coffee than a straight shot.

nuance.analogy: It is like a shot of espresso stretched into a full mug, similar to a thinned-out version of the same ingredient.
nuance.etymology: From Italian americano, meaning 'American'; the popular story about US soldiers in WWII diluting espresso is folklore and not well documented.
common_mistakes: Stressing MAIR as in 'AMERica' instead of KAH at the end of the word.
Ordering 'Americano coffee', which is redundant because the drink is already coffee.
Confusing the coffee drink with the Campari cocktail of the same name when a bartender is speaking.

americano.etymology: 1970s, from Italian *caffè americano* or American Spanish *americano* (“American”).

conversation.text: I'll have a hot americano with a little milk.
An americano is just espresso with hot water.
Can I get a large iced americano?

senses.definition: A religious article, protective charm, or ornament, usually bearing cultural or magical symbols, worn for protection against ill will, negative influences, the evil eye, or evil spirits.
senses.example: The soldier wore an amulet for protection.

core.definition: A small object, often worn on a cord or chain, believed to protect its wearer from harm, bad luck or evil spirits.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllables are quick and reduced, and the final -et is a soft, unstressed 'uht,' not a full 'let.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests protection and good fortune, but it can also carry a sense of superstition, depending on the speaker's beliefs.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use amulet mostly when describing jewelry, folk traditions, religious or cultural objects, museum exhibits or stories. In everyday talk they say 'lucky charm,' 'good luck charm' or 'evil eye necklace.' Calling a religious object an amulet can sound dismissive to some believers, so describe it respectfully when talking to them.

distinctions.note: A talisman is often described as having magical power, especially in fiction or folklore. An amulet is more commonly a protective object worn on the body.
A charm is a small ornament, often a bracelet piece, for luck or decoration. An amulet is more specifically meant for protection against harm.
A relic is a physical remnant of a saint or sacred figure, venerated for holiness. An amulet is a protective object, not necessarily connected to a saint.

examples.everyday: My sister wears a little blue evil-eye amulet on her necklace for good luck.
examples.professional: The museum's curator labeled the Egyptian amulet with its date, material and the place where it was found.
examples.analytical: Many amulets combine Christian and folk symbols, which makes it hard to draw a sharp line between devotion and magical protection.

nuance.analogy: Like a seatbelt for the spirit: you do not expect a crash, but you wear it anyway.
nuance.etymology: From Latin amuletum, of uncertain origin, possibly from a Semitic or Greek source.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'omelet' because the spellings look alike; the words are pronounced very differently.
Stressing the last syllable, as in am-yuh-LET.
Saying 'AM-yoo-let' with a full vowel in the last syllable instead of a reduced ending.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, based on, or composed of an analogy.

core.definition: Based on or involving analogy; reasoning by comparing cases that are similar in some relevant way.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on LAH, the third syllable. The a in LAH is a broad open vowel, like the a in 'father'. Learners often stress the first syllable, saying AN-uh-lah-jih-kul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical adjective with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Used in logic, science, law, and education to describe reasoning that compares cases. Americans say analogical reasoning in teaching and psychology, but in everyday talk they say 'it's like' or 'by comparison'. The adjective is formal, so keep it for academic writing; using it in casual conversation sounds stiff.

distinctions.note: Analogical describes reasoning or methods based on analogy; analogous describes two things that resemble each other in a relevant way.
Deductive reasoning moves from general premises to a guaranteed conclusion; analogical reasoning moves from one case to a similar one, so the conclusion is only probable.

examples.everyday: My uncle explained the stock market with an analogical story about a garden, which made it easy to follow.
examples.professional: The team used analogical reasoning to adapt the fraud model from credit cards to insurance claims.
examples.analytical: An analogical argument is only as strong as the relevant similarities it identifies between the two cases.

nuance.analogy: Like using a map of one city to find your way around a similar city.
nuance.etymology: From analogy, from Greek analogia, 'proportion', with the adjective suffix -ical.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as AN-uh-log-ical.
Confusing analogical (based on analogy) with analogous (similar to something).

senses.definition: Causing anesthesia; reducing pain sensitivity.
Insensate: unable to feel, or unconscious.
A substance administered to reduce the perception of pain or to induce numbness for surgery and may render the recipient unconscious.

core.definition: A drug that numbs pain or causes loss of feeling or consciousness, used during surgery or dental work.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on THEH, the third syllable. The first syllable is an, the second is a reduced uh, and the last syllable is a short i like in 'tick.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and medical, though the word may remind people of pain relief or a procedure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say anesthetic for the drug or for an adjective describing something that numbs, such as 'an anesthetic cream.' In a dentist's office people often say 'numbing shot' or 'the numbing medicine.' When discussing surgery, a doctor may say 'anesthesia' for the general process and 'anesthetic' for the specific drug.

distinctions.note: Anesthesia is the process or state of blocking sensation, while anesthetic is the specific substance that causes it.
An analgesic relieves pain without necessarily causing numbness or unconsciousness, while an anesthetic blocks sensation more fully.

examples.everyday: The dentist put a numbing gel on my gum, and it was the same kind of anesthetic they use before a shot.
examples.professional: Let's confirm the anesthetic dose with pharmacy before the procedure is added to the schedule.
examples.analytical: The trial compares a novel anesthetic against standard agents on recovery time and postoperative nausea.

nuance.analogy: An anesthetic is like a dimmer switch for feeling: it turns down sensation until the signal is too faint to reach the brain as pain.
nuance.etymology: From Greek an-, without, and aisthesis, sensation, with the -etic ending added in English.
common_mistakes: Confusing anesthetic with antiseptic, which kills germs rather than numbing pain.
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable as 'AN-es-thet-ic.'

anesthetic.etymology: From *an* + *esthetic*, or Latinized form of *grc:ἀναίσθητος* + *ic*, from *ἀν-* (“un-”) + *αἰσθητικός* (“perceptible”).

senses.definition: The study of angels. Angels have been grouped into nine categories or “choirs,” from lowest to highest: angel, archangel, principality, power, virtue, dominion, throne, cherub, and seraph.

core.definition: The branch of theology that studies angels, including their nature, ranks and role in God's plan.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the fourth-from-last syllable, LAH, like other -ology words. The first syllable is 'an' as in 'angel', not 'ayn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and scholarly.
nuance.usage_note: Used in theology and religious studies. It names both the discipline and a particular system of belief about angels. Casual speakers would say 'what the Bible says about angels'.

distinctions.note: Demonology studies demons and fallen angels; angelology studies angels, often including the fallen.
Christology studies the person and work of Christ, not angels.
Eschatology studies last things; angelology studies angels, though they overlap in end-times texts.

examples.everyday: I'm taking a class on angelology, and we're reading what the Bible says about angels.
examples.professional: The seminar introduces students to angelology, from Scripture to Pseudo-Dionysius.
examples.analytical: Dionysius's angelology arranges the heavenly beings in three triads, shaping Christian thought for centuries.

nuance.etymology: From Greek angelos (messenger) + -logia (study of).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'ayn' instead of 'an'.
Stressing the wrong syllable instead of LAH.
Confusing it with demonology.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek angelos and Hebrew mal'ak both mean 'messenger'. Angels appear in Isaiah 6:1-7, where seraphim attend God's throne, and in Luke 1:26-38, where Gabriel announces Jesus' birth to Mary. Hebrews 1:14 describes angels as ministering spirits sent to serve those who inherit salvation. The nine-choir ranking comes from Pseudo-Dionysius, not from the Bible itself.

senses.definition: A collection of literary works, such as poems or short stories, especially a collection from various authors.
A work or series containing various stories with no direct relation to one another.
An assortment of things.
The study of flowers.

core.definition: A published collection of literary works, such as poems or short stories, usually from several authors.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, THOL, with an 'ah' vowel as in 'hot.' The ending -ogy is pronounced 'uh-jee,' not 'o-lo-gee.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests quality, variety, and a curated selection.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use anthology for a book that gathers stories, poems, or essays, often in English or literature classes. It can also describe a collection of songs or TV episodes in casual talk. A single book by one author is not an anthology, so do not use the word for that.

distinctions.note: Collection is general and can refer to anything gathered. Anthology usually means a published selection of literary works.
Compilation is broader and often refers to music or data gathered from many sources. Anthology is more literary and curated.

examples.everyday: I bought an anthology of short stories to read on the plane.
examples.professional: We're publishing an anthology of case studies from our customer success team next quarter.
examples.analytical: The volume is less a simple anthology than a curated argument, since each essay responds to the others.

nuance.analogy: Like a playlist of stories: each piece stands alone, but the selection shows a particular taste.
nuance.etymology: From Greek anthologia, 'flower gathering,' from anthos 'flower' and legein 'to gather.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as long o, as in an-THOL-o-gee.
Using anthology for a single book by one author.
Confusing anthology with anthem, which is a song.

anthology.etymology: Ancient Greek *ἀνθολογία* (“flower-gathering”), from *ἀνθολογέω* (“I gather flowers”), from *ἄνθος* (“flower”) + *λέγω* (“I gather, pick up, collect”), coined by Meleager of Gadara circa 60 BCE, originally as Στέφανος (*στέφανος* (“garland”)) to describe a…

senses.definition: Regardless; anyhow.
senses.example: He didn't enjoy washing his car, but it was so dirty that he did it anyway.

senses.definition: Used to indicate that a statement explains or supports a previous statement. See anyhow and at least.
senses.example: I don't think that's true. I haven't found any evidence, anyway.

senses.definition: Used to indicate a change of subject.
Used at the end of a question for emphasis, or to direct the conversation to something of more broad importance (compare with more to the point).

core.definition: Despite what was just said; in any case. Also used to change the subject or return to the main point.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the second word 'way' strong but short. The middle is a reduced 'nee', so do not say 'an-ee-WAY'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound dismissive if used to cut someone off, but is often just a friendly way to move on.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'anyway' constantly in conversation to shift topics ('Anyway, what I wanted to say...') or to end a story ('Anyway, that's how I got the car.'). It also means 'despite that', as in 'It's late, but anyway, let's go.' In formal writing, 'in any case' or 'regardless' is preferred.

distinctions.note: Nearly identical in meaning; anyhow is slightly more regional or casual.
However sets up a formal contrast, while anyway often dismisses an objection or shifts the topic.
Formal and precise, suited to reports and emails rather than casual talk.

examples.everyday: Anyway, I should get going before the traffic gets bad.
examples.professional: Anyway, the vendor missed the deadline, so let's move to the next item on the agenda.
examples.analytical: Anyway signals that the speaker grants an objection without accepting its consequences, a move that keeps the argument moving forward.

nuance.analogy: Like stepping around a puddle and continuing on your walk.
nuance.etymology: From 'any' and 'way', originally meaning 'in any way'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'any way' as two words when you mean 'regardless', which changes the meaning.
Starting every sentence with 'Anyway' in essays, which sounds like a spoken filler.

conversation.text: Anyway, like I was saying, the trip was amazing.
Anyway, I should let you get back to work.
It was raining, but we went to the beach anyway.

senses.definition: To move upward, to fly, to soar.
senses.example: He ascended to heaven upon a cloud.

senses.definition: To slope in an upward direction.
To go up.
senses.example: You ascend the stairs and take a right.

senses.definition: To succeed a ruler on (the throne).
senses.example: She ascended the throne when her mother abdicated.

senses.definition: To rise; to become higher, more noble, etc.
To trace, search or go backwards temporally (e.g. through records, genealogies, routes, etc.).
senses.example: Our inquiries ascend to the remotest antiquity.

senses.definition: To cease being an incel, generally by losing one's virginity and engaging in sexual intercourse, or by forming a romantic relationship.
To become higher in pitch.

core.definition: To move upward or climb up to a higher place, level, or position.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SEND, and the first vowel is a reduced schwa. Don't say 'AS-end'; the d at the end is a clear, voiced sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds more formal or elevated than 'go up' or 'climb', so it suits written or careful speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ascend' mostly in formal writing, news, and speeches, such as 'the plane began to ascend' or 'the stairs ascend to the second floor.' In casual talk they say 'go up,' 'climb,' or 'rise.' Its best-known everyday use is in phrases like 'ascend the throne' or 'ascend to power.'

distinctions.note: 'Climb' suggests effort with hands and feet, while 'ascend' is neutral about effort and is more formal.
'Rise' is general and common in everyday speech, while 'ascend' stresses a gradual, deliberate upward movement.
'Descend' is the direct opposite, meaning to move downward.

examples.everyday: We had to ascend three flights of stairs to get to the apartment, so bring only what you need.
examples.professional: The team's latency metric began to ascend after the last deployment, so we need to roll it back.
examples.analytical: For Plato, the soul must ascend from the changing world of appearances toward the unchanging Forms.

nuance.analogy: Think of a hot-air balloon slowly lifting off the ground, rising steadily in a controlled way.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ascendere, 'to climb up,' from ad- 'to' plus scandere 'to climb.'
common_mistakes: Using 'ascend' for everyday climbing, which sounds stiff; say 'go up' or 'climb' instead.
Saying 'AS-end' with stress on the first syllable instead of the second.

ascend.etymology: From Middle English *ascenden*, borrowed from Old French *ascendre*, from Latin *ascendō* (“to go up, climb up to”), from *ad* (“to”) + *scandō* (“to climb”); see *scan*.

senses.definition: The praxis or "exercise" of asceticism and self-denial of impulses or passions for the sake of piety, theosis, and connection with God.
(Rigorous) self-discipline, particularly as a religious observance; asceticism.

core.definition: Disciplined spiritual self-training, including fasting and self-denial, undertaken to grow in holiness and union with God.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SEE, and the final syllables are short and unstressed. Don't say 'ass-EE-sis' with a hard a at the start; the first vowel is a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in religious contexts, serious and admiring; can sound severe to outsiders.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ascesis' almost only in theology, church history, Orthodox writing, and religious studies. In ordinary conversation, people would say 'self-discipline,' 'discipline,' or 'asceticism.' The word can be confused with 'askesis' in older texts, but the spelling 'ascesis' is standard in English theology.

distinctions.note: 'Asceticism' names the whole practice or lifestyle, while 'ascesis' often names the disciplined exercise or training itself, especially in Eastern Orthodox use.
'Self-discipline' is a general everyday term for control over behavior, while 'ascesis' is a religious term aimed at spiritual growth.

examples.everyday: My friend who goes to the Orthodox church said that fasting is a form of ascesis that helps her pray.
examples.professional: In our parish course, the instructor described ascesis as the training that prepares the heart for prayer.
examples.analytical: Orthodox writers treat ascesis not as an end in itself but as a means of purifying the nous so that the soul may be united with God.

nuance.analogy: Ascesis is like an athlete's training: regular, disciplined effort that shapes the body and mind for a specific goal.
nuance.etymology: From Greek askēsis, 'exercise, training,' from askein 'to work, exercise.'
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it as 'ass-EE-sis'; the stress is on the first syllable of the main root, SEE.
Using 'ascesis' in everyday speech where 'self-discipline' would be natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word askēsis means training or exercise, especially athletic training. Paul uses the athletic image in 1 Corinthians 9:25-27, where he disciplines his body to avoid disqualification. In 1 Timothy 4:7-8 he tells Timothy to train himself for godliness, noting that bodily training is of some value but godliness is of value in every way.

ascesis.etymology: Late Latin *ascesis*, or directly from its etymon, Ancient Greek *ἄσκησις* (“exercise, training”), from *ἀσκέω* (“to exercise, practise, train”) + *-σῐς*.

senses.definition: The act of assimilating or the state of being assimilated.
The metabolic conversion of nutrients into tissue.
The absorption of new ideas into an existing cognitive structure.
A sound change process by which the phonetics of a speech segment becomes more like that of another segment in a word (or at a word boundary), so that a change of phoneme occurs.
The adoption, by a minority group, of the customs and attitudes of the dominant culture.
senses.example: After centuries of British cultural assimilation, a majority of Irish now speak English instead of Irish.

core.definition: The process of absorbing a person, group, or new information into an existing culture, system, or mind.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LAY, and the -tion ending is pronounced 'shun'. The middle syllables are quick and reduced, not 'ah-sim-ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in science and learning, but sensitive in social discussions because it can suggest pressure to give up original identity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use assimilation mostly in discussions of immigration, education, or sociology. In biology or nutrition it is a technical term for absorbing nutrients. In casual talk, people more often say 'fitting in' or 'settling in'.

distinctions.note: Integration joins a group while keeping its identity; assimilation suggests the newcomer adopts the dominant culture fully.
Acculturation describes adopting a new culture and is often seen as two-way; assimilation is often seen as one-directional.
Adaptation means changing behavior to fit conditions; assimilation means absorbing something new into existing structures.

examples.everyday: My grandparents talked a lot about assimilation when they first moved to Chicago.
examples.professional: The team tracked the assimilation of new hires by measuring how quickly they closed their first pull requests.
examples.analytical: Assimilation theories in sociology often assume a single direction, from immigrant to host culture, which the evidence does not fully support.

nuance.analogy: Like a river absorbing a tributary: the water changes, and the tributary becomes part of the flow.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin assimilatio, from assimilare, to make like.
common_mistakes: Saying 'assimilation to' when the usual phrase is 'assimilation into' a society or culture.
Confusing assimilation with 'simulation', which means a model or imitation of something.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to, or exhibiting strict obedience to an authority; favoring authoritarianism over civic and individual liberties.
senses.example: the authoritarian personality

senses.definition: Demanding obedience to authority; marked by authoritarianism; dictatorial, tyrannical.
senses.example: The authoritarian government was demanding stricter laws for low-wage peasants.

senses.definition: Tending to impose one's demands upon others as if one were an authority.
One who commands absolute obedience to his or her authority.
senses.example: The dictator was an authoritarian.

senses.definition: One who follows and is excessively obedient to authority.

core.definition: Demanding strict obedience to authority and rejecting individual freedoms, dissent, or challenges to those in power.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TAIR, the fourth syllable, and the -ian ending is a weak 'un', not 'ee-an'. Keep a clear r after the o in thor, since Americans pronounce it fully.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes controlling, oppressive behavior by governments or leaders, and it is an insult when used for a boss or parent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use authoritarian mainly for governments, political movements, and sometimes strict parenting or management styles. In everyday talk, 'bossy' or 'controlling' is more common, so authoritarian can sound heavy or political. Calling a manager authoritarian in a meeting will be taken seriously.

distinctions.note: Authoritative means reliable or commanding respect for expertise; authoritarian means demanding obedience and suppressing freedom. The two are often confused.
Autocratic focuses on one person ruling with unchecked decision-making; authoritarian focuses on demanding obedience and crushing dissent.
Bossy is informal and describes an annoying personal habit, while authoritarian is a stronger, more formal description of a system or style.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's boss is so authoritarian that nobody on his team dares to speak up.
examples.professional: Our manager's authoritarian approach to code reviews is discouraging people from asking questions.
examples.analytical: Scholars of political theory often argue that authoritarian rule depends less on ideology than on the suppression of public debate.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who won't let any player question a call, even when the call is clearly wrong.
nuance.etymology: From French autoritaire, from autorité, 'authority', from Latin auctoritas.
common_mistakes: Confusing authoritarian with authoritative, which has a positive meaning about expertise or reliability.
Using authoritarian as a compliment about someone who leads well.
Stressing the wrong syllable, such as au-thor-ih-TAIR-ee-un with a weak final vowel.

senses.definition: Lacking social skills, or uncomfortable with social interaction.
senses.example: I'm very awkward at parties.

senses.definition: Perverse; adverse; difficult to handle.
senses.example: He's a right awkward chap.

senses.definition: Lacking dexterity in the use of the hands or of tools.
senses.example: John was awkward at performing the trick. He'll have to practice to improve.

senses.definition: Not easily managed; embarrassing.
senses.example: That was an extremely awkward moment. Everyone was watching.

senses.definition: Someone or something that is awkward.

core.definition: Causing or feeling social embarrassment or discomfort; not smooth, natural, or easy to handle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the final syllable as a reduced werd with an r sound, not wahrd or ward. The k and w sounds blend quickly, so say them together without a pause.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. It describes discomfort or a clumsy moment; describing a person as awkward can sound unkind.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use awkward constantly for small social moments: That was so awkward, an awkward question, I feel awkward. It can describe a person who seems socially unsure, but saying that directly can be impolite. A natural reply is Yeah, super awkward, or Ha, it's okay.

distinctions.note: Uncomfortable can describe physical or emotional discomfort; awkward focuses on social tension or a situation that is hard to handle.
Clumsy describes physical movements or handling things; awkward can describe a social situation or someone's unsure manner.
Embarrassing focuses on shame or humiliation; awkward focuses on tension or not knowing how to act.

examples.everyday: I accidentally called my neighbor by the wrong name, and it was so awkward.
examples.professional: It's awkward to bring up the budget cut in front of the client, so let's talk about it after the meeting.
examples.analytical: Awkward moments reveal the unwritten norms that govern how people expect one another to behave.

nuance.analogy: Like a chair that is slightly the wrong height: nothing is broken, but nothing fits comfortably.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English awkeward, meaning 'turned the wrong way', from Old Norse afug 'turned backward' plus -ward.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as two words, AW-k WARD, or dropping the w; it is one word with a quick k-w sound.
Calling a shy person awkward to their face; it can sound insulting, so describe the situation instead.

conversation.text: It was awkward running into my ex at the store.
I felt so awkward at the party because I didn't know anyone.
Three o'clock is an awkward time for a meeting; I'll be picking up the kids.
It was so awkward when I called him by the wrong name.
Things got awkward when they started talking about politics.
I'm always a little awkward around new people.
This box is awkward to carry. Can you grab one end?

senses.definition: An order that cannot be currently filled or shipped, but is requested nonetheless for when the item becomes available again.
senses.example: on backorder

senses.definition: To place such an order.

core.definition: An order placed for an item that is out of stock, which will be shipped once the item becomes available again.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on BACK. The middle syllable is the open or sound, and the last syllable is a reduced er, not ORD-er with stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a factual shopping term, though it can frustrate customers who need the item soon.
nuance.usage_note: Americans see this most in online shopping, as in 'This item is on backorder and will ship in three weeks.' People also say 'it's backordered' as an adjective. If an item is on backorder, ask for a firm delivery date or check whether you can cancel without penalty.

distinctions.note: A preorder is for an item not yet released. A backorder is for an item that was available before but is now out of stock.
Out of stock means unavailable now and possibly with no order option. Backorder means you can still order it for later delivery.
A waitlist is for limited items where you wait your turn. A backorder is placed now and shipped when stock returns.

examples.everyday: The store said the blender is on backorder, so it won't ship for three weeks.
examples.professional: Two of our SKUs are backordered from the supplier, so we need to revise the Q3 fulfillment forecast.
examples.analytical: A backorder is a commitment to a customer despite constrained supply, which shifts the risk from inventory to delivery promises.

nuance.analogy: Like booking a table at a restaurant that is full tonight but has a seat next week.
nuance.etymology: From back plus order, meaning an order held back until the goods are available again.
common_mistakes: Saying the item is in backorder instead of on backorder.
Confusing backorder with preorder for a new release.
Stressing ORDER in the second part. The main stress is on BACK.

conversation.text: The desk is on backorder, so it won't ship until next month.
My shoes were on backorder for three weeks, but they finally shipped.
How long is the backorder on this item?

senses.definition: Any of various aromatic resins exuded from certain plants, especially trees of the genus Commiphora of Africa, Arabia and India and Myroxylon of South America.
An aromatic preparation for embalming the dead.
A plant or tree yielding such substance.
Any soothing oil or lotion, especially an aromatic one.
Something soothing.
senses.example: Classical music is a sweet balm for our sorrows.

senses.definition: The lemon balm, Melissa officinalis.
Any of a number of other aromatic herbs with a similar citrus-like scent, such as bee balm and horsebalm.
To soothe; to mitigate.

core.definition: A soothing ointment or substance for the skin, or something that comforts and relieves pain or stress.

pronunciation.tip: The L is silent, and the vowel is the open ah of father, not the aw of bomb. Say it as a single syllable that rhymes with calm, not with palm.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests comfort and healing, and it is often used figuratively for emotional relief.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people mainly say lip balm for a waxy product used on dry lips. The figurative use, such as a balm for the soul, sounds literary and is common in sermons, poetry and thoughtful writing. A natural reply to a gift of lip balm is Thanks, I really needed that.

distinctions.note: Ointment is a medical term for a thicker healing preparation applied to skin.
Salve is an older-fashioned word for a healing ointment and sounds archaic in modern American speech.
Lotion is thinner and used mainly for moisturizing, while balm is often used to soothe or protect.

examples.everyday: Can you pass me the lip balm? My lips are so dry from this cold wind.
examples.professional: A short walk and a cup of coffee was a balm after the three-hour outage review.
examples.analytical: For the psalmist, prayer becomes a balm for the anxious soul, a comfort that is not merely emotional but relational.

nuance.analogy: A balm is like cool water on a sunburn; it does not remove the cause, but it makes the pain easier to bear.
nuance.etymology: From Old French basme, from Latin balsamum, from Greek balsamon, probably of Semitic origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the L, as in bolm or balm with a clear L; the L is silent.
Confusing balm with palm, the tree or the hand part, because the spelling and sound are close.
Using balm only for medicine when Americans also use it figuratively for comfort.

balm.etymology: Middle English *bawme*, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Middle French *baume*, from Old French *basme*, from Latin *balsamum*, itself from Ancient Greek *βάλσαμον*.

senses.definition: To perform the sacrament of baptism by immersing someone in water or sprinkling or pouring water over them.
To Christianize.
To dedicate or christen.
To ensure proper burning of a joint by moistening the exterior with saliva.
To extinguish the life of.

core.definition: To administer the Christian sacrament of baptism, using water, as a sign of cleansing, new life, and entry into the church.

pronunciation.tip: American stress falls on the second syllable: bap-TYZE. The noun baptism shifts stress to the first syllable: BAP-tiz-um. The ending is a voiced /z/, not /s/.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; deeply meaningful within Christian communities. Used figuratively ("baptized by fire") it suggests a harsh first experience.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use baptize mostly in church contexts: parents baptize babies, or pastors baptize believers. Baptists and many evangelicals say a person is baptized after professing faith. Figurative uses like "a baptism by fire" are common in ordinary talk about a tough initiation.

distinctions.note: Christen is more informal and often refers to naming a baby at baptism, or humorously to naming a ship or first use of something.
Immerse describes only the physical act of dipping fully into liquid and has no religious meaning by itself.
Dedicate means to commit a person or thing to a purpose; Baptists "dedicate" infants without baptizing them.

collocations: be baptized in the name of

examples.everyday: We're getting our daughter baptized at church next Sunday, and you're welcome to come.
examples.professional: The pastor will baptize six new members during the Easter service.
examples.analytical: Churches differ over whether to baptize infants or only those who can profess faith for themselves.

nuance.analogy: To baptize is like a public initiation ceremony, where water marks a person as belonging to a new community.
nuance.etymology: From Greek baptizein, "to dip or immerse," via Latin baptizare and Old French.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (BAP-tize) instead of bap-TYZE.
Saying the ending with /s/ instead of /z/.
Using it as a noun; the noun is baptism.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb is baptizō, "to dip, immerse." In Matthew 3:13-17, Jesus is baptized by John in the Jordan, with the Spirit descending. In Matthew 28:19, Jesus commands the disciples to baptize all nations in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In Acts 2:38, Peter calls the crowd to repent and be baptized for the forgiveness of sins.

traditions.view: Baptism is a mystery (sacrament) performed by triple immersion, usually of infants, and is followed immediately by chrismation and communion. It cleanses and incorporates the person into the Church.
Baptism is the first sacrament, usually given to infants by pouring water with the Trinitarian formula. It removes original sin and makes one a member of the Church.

Lutherans, Anglicans, and Reformed baptize infants, seeing baptism as a means or sign of grace and covenant. Baptists and many Pentecostals baptize only believers, by immersion, as a public witness and ordinance rather than a saving sacrament.

baptize.etymology: From Middle English *baptisen*, *baptizen*, from Old French *baptiser*, *batisier*, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin *baptizo*, from Ancient Greek *βαπτίζω* (“to immerse, plunge, baptize”).

senses.definition: Of or relating to a barbarian; uncivilized, uncultured or uncouth.
senses.example: a barbaric attack on a doctor in a hospital

core.definition: Extremely cruel, brutal or uncivilized; very harsh or unacceptable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable. The 'r' sounds are clear in both places, and the final 'ic' is a short 'ik'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It condemns cruelty or extreme conduct, so it is strong language and should be used carefully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'barbaric' to express strong disapproval, for example about cruel treatment or outrageous rules: 'That policy is barbaric.' It can sound dramatic in casual talk, so many people prefer 'brutal' or 'cruel'. A natural reply is 'I agree, that's awful.'

distinctions.note: 'Brutal' describes physical violence or harshness. 'Barbaric' also condemns the act as uncivilized.
'Uncivilized' is a general term for a lack of culture or order. 'Barbaric' is a stronger moral judgment.

examples.everyday: Making kids work twelve-hour days without breaks is barbaric, if you ask me.
examples.professional: Requiring employees to answer messages at midnight is a barbaric practice that hurts morale.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that describing an enemy as barbaric can justify cruelty by denying the enemy full humanity.

nuance.analogy: Like a rule that treats people as objects instead of humans.
nuance.etymology: From Latin barbaricus, from Greek barbarikos, 'foreign', from barbaros, 'non-Greek speaker'.
common_mistakes: Using it for mild disagreement; it is a strong word for serious cruelty.
Stressing the first syllable; stress is on the second.

barbaric.etymology: Inherited from Middle English *barbarik*, from Old French *barbarique* (“barbarous”), from Latin *barbaricus*, from Ancient Greek *βαρβαρικός* (“barbaric, savage, fierce”), from *βάρβαρος* + *-ικός*.

core.definition: The Babylonian god, whose name means "lord," a title of Marduk; the Bible portrays him as a powerless false idol.

pronunciation.tip: It sounds exactly like the word "bell." Do not add a vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative in biblical usage, as the name of a false god; neutral in historical writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans meet Bel mostly in Bible study and in Old Testament scholarship. It is not an everyday word. Because it sounds like "bell," spoken context matters.

distinctions.note: Baal is the Canaanite storm and fertility god; Bel is the Babylonian form of the same title "lord."
Marduk is the personal name of Babylon's chief god; Bel is his title.
Nebo is Bel's son in Babylonian religion, and the two appear together in Isaiah 46.

examples.everyday: We read in Isaiah that Bel, the Babylonian god, bows down and cannot save anyone.
examples.professional: In my lecture on exile, I'll show how the prophets mock Bel as a lifeless idol.
examples.analytical: Isaiah 46 contrasts Bel, carried on beasts of burden, with a God who carries his people.

nuance.analogy: Calling Marduk "Bel" is like calling a king "My Lord" until the title becomes the name.
nuance.etymology: From Akkadian Belu, from a Semitic root meaning "lord," related to Hebrew Baal.
common_mistakes: Confusing Bel with the Canaanite Baal.
Spelling it "Bell."
nuance.biblical_note: Bel is the Babylonian equivalent of Hebrew Baal, "lord." Isaiah 46:1 says Bel bows down and Nebo stoops, as their idols are carried off on beasts. Jeremiah 50:2 announces that Bel is put to shame and Marduk dismayed when Babylon falls. Jeremiah 51:44 says God will punish Bel in Babylon. Bel and the Dragon is an addition to Daniel in the Apocrypha.

senses.definition: Warlike or combative in nature; aggressively hostile.
senses.example: You don't have to be so bellicose, and we can work out a peaceful solution.

core.definition: Eager to fight or argue; aggressively hostile and warlike in attitude or behavior.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on the first syllable, BEL. The ending -cose is pronounced like the word cows, with a final s sound, not a z.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes aggression and a readiness to fight, often in leaders, rhetoric, or personalities.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bellicose mainly in news, political commentary, and formal writing, usually about nations, leaders, or hostile rhetoric. In everyday speech, people more often say aggressive, combative, or spoiling for a fight. Calling a person bellicose can sound harsh and pointed, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Bellicose emphasizes a warlike temperament or tone, while belligerent often describes actual hostile conduct, sometimes including open conflict.
Aggressive is a common everyday word for forceful behavior. Bellicose is stronger, more formal, and suggests a readiness for war or conflict.

examples.everyday: Dan gets pretty bellicose after a couple of beers, so I try to steer clear of politics with him.
examples.professional: The vendor's bellicose tone in the meeting made it almost impossible to negotiate the contract.
examples.analytical: Realist theorists argue that bellicose rhetoric among states often reflects a security dilemma rather than pure aggression.

nuance.analogy: A bellicose person is like a dog that growls at every passerby, always ready to bark or bite before anyone has done anything.
nuance.etymology: From Latin bellicosus, warlike, from bellicus of war, from bellum war.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in bel-LICK-ose.
Using it for a mild disagreement; it is too strong for ordinary arguments.

core.definition: Ancient town north of Jerusalem, meaning 'house of God'; where Jacob dreamed of a ladder to heaven and named the place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BETH, and the second syllable is a light, reduced 'uhl', not a full 'ell'. The 'th' is the voiceless sound in 'thin'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in religious use, where it means a place of God's presence; neutral as a place name or town name.
nuance.usage_note: Bethel is a proper noun, so write it with a capital letter. Americans know it mainly from the Bible or from church names such as Bethel Baptist Church. Many U.S. towns and churches are called Bethel, often after the biblical place, so if the context is unclear, ask which Bethel is meant.

distinctions.note: Bethel is the place where Jacob met God in Genesis; Bethlehem is the town in Judah where David and Jesus were born. Do not mix them up.

collocations: the house of God at Bethel

examples.everyday: We're meeting for lunch at the Bethel Church fellowship hall after the service.
examples.professional: The Bethel campus conference room is booked until three, so let's move the review to the main building.
examples.analytical: Jacob's naming of Bethel as the house of God shows how Genesis ties divine revelation to particular places and to the promises made there.

nuance.analogy: Like a sign on a road that says 'God was here', a name that marks the spot where someone met God.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew bêt-ʾēl, 'house of God'.
common_mistakes: Confusing Bethel with Bethlehem, which is a different town in Judah.
Saying 'BETH-ELL' with a full second vowel instead of a reduced 'uhl'.
nuance.biblical_note: Bethel is Hebrew bêt-ʾēl, 'house of God'; the place was earlier called Luz, and Genesis 28:19 says Jacob renamed it Bethel. Genesis 28:10-22 tells of Jacob's dream of a ladder at Bethel and his vow. Genesis 35:6-15 describes God appearing to Jacob there again and confirming his new name Israel. 1 Kings 12:28-29 reports that Jeroboam set up a golden calf at Bethel, which made it a rival worship center that prophets such as Amos (Amos 7:13) condemned.

senses.definition: The balance between error from overly simple models (bias) and error from overly sensitive ones (variance).

core.definition: The balance between error from overly simple models (high bias) and error from overly sensitive models that fit noise (high variance).

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'BY' in bias and on 'TRADE' in tradeoff, while 'variance' has a weaker secondary stress on VAIR. The final -ance is a reduced 'uhns', and the 'trade-off' compound is often said as one smooth phrase, 'TRAYD-off'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes an unavoidable balance rather than a fault.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and machine learning engineers use this phrase in model reviews, courses, and papers, and it often comes up in meetings about model complexity. Americans write it as 'bias-variance tradeoff' or 'bias-variance trade-off', and both are accepted. Outside technical work, most people won't know it, so explain it briefly with 'model too simple versus too sensitive'.

distinctions.note: Overfitting is one symptom of high variance, where a model memorizes noise in the training data; the tradeoff describes the whole balance.
Underfitting is typically high bias, where a model is too simple to capture the real pattern.

examples.everyday: My cousin who studies data science keeps going on about the bias-variance tradeoff, and I still don't get it.
examples.professional: We simplified the model to reduce variance, but that raised bias, so we need to find the right point on the bias-variance tradeoff.
examples.analytical: Every choice of model complexity sits somewhere on the bias-variance tradeoff, so no learning method escapes error entirely.

nuance.analogy: Like tuning a guitar string, tighten it too little and the note is flat, tighten it too much and it wobbles with every touch.
nuance.etymology: Bias comes from French biais, 'slant'; variance comes from Latin variantia, 'difference'; the compound is a modern technical term.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'variance' as the main beat, as in 'vair-ee-AHNS'; the main stress is on the bias and tradeoff parts.
Thinking the tradeoff means you can eliminate both errors; the point is to balance them.
Saying 'bias-variance trade-off' with the stress on 'off' instead of 'TRADE'.

conversation.text: The bias-variance tradeoff describes how simpler models err systematically while complex models are sensitive to the training sample.
Deeper trees cut bias but raised variance, so we picked a middle depth: the bias-variance tradeoff in action.
Double descent complicates the classic bias-variance tradeoff story for very large models.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to something containing or consisting of bile.
Resembling bile, especially in color.
Peevishly ill-humored, irritable or bad tempered; irascible.
Suffering from real or supposed liver disorder, especially excessive secretions of bile.

core.definition: Feeling sick to the stomach, nauseated, or unpleasantly irritable and bad-tempered, as in a 'bilious' mood.

pronunciation.tip: Drop the middle syllable so the word has only two syllables, with the -ious ending sounding like 'yus' and not 'ee-us'. The stress falls on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The word describes unpleasant physical or emotional states and sounds old-fashioned or literary in modern speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say bilious in everyday conversation. You are more likely to hear 'queasy' or 'nauseous' for feeling sick, or 'grouchy' for being irritable. You will see bilious in older novels, reviews and descriptive writing, where it often describes a sickly greenish color or a sour, sullen mood.

distinctions.note: Queasy describes a mild, everyday feeling of nausea, while bilious sounds more literary and can also describe a sour temper.
Nauseous is the common everyday word for feeling sick to the stomach, though many grammarians prefer 'nauseated' for this sense.

examples.everyday: I ate too much pizza last night and I still feel kind of bilious this morning.
examples.professional: The client's reply was so bilious that our whole team went quiet during the call.
examples.analytical: The critic's bilious prose reveals more about his own resentment than about the novel he claims to dismiss.

nuance.analogy: A bilious mood is like a sour lemon: bitter, sharp and hard to be around.
nuance.etymology: From Latin biliosus, 'full of bile', from bilis, 'bile'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as three syllables, 'bil-ee-us', instead of two.
Using bilious as a neutral synonym for 'sick' in everyday speech, where it sounds stiff or literary.

bilious.etymology: From French *bilieux*, from Latin *bīliōsus* (“full of bile”), from *bīlis* (“bile”) + *-ōsus* (“full of”).

senses.definition: A small casual restaurant or pub, typically serving French-style cuisine.
(rare) To eat at a bistro.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A small, casual restaurant, often serving simple French-style food and wine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable with a long e: BEE-stroh, not BIS-tro with a short i. The r in the second syllable is clear, and the final vowel is a plain oh sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it suggests a cozy, relaxed place that feels a bit nicer than a diner or cafe.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bistro for a casual but slightly upscale restaurant with a small menu, often in a city neighborhood. Many restaurants call themselves bistros even when they serve American food, so the word signals atmosphere more than cuisine.
