senses.example: They recovered three of the explorers very much alive, then another, wracked with severe hypothermia, who was taken to hospital.

senses.definition: To replenish to, resume (a good state of mind or body).
senses.example: At the top of the hill I asked to stop for a few minutes to recover my strength.

senses.definition: To obtain a positive judgment; to win in a lawsuit.
senses.example: The plaintiff recovered in his suit, being awarded declaratory relief and a clearing of his name.

senses.definition: To regain one's composure, balance etc.
senses.example: Spinning round, he caught a stone with his ankle, but recovered quickly before turning to face me.

senses.definition: To get better, to regain health or prosperity.
senses.example: I was hurt, but I knew I’d recover, given time.

senses.definition: To cover again.
To add a new roof membrane or steep-slope covering over an existing one.
To gain as compensation or reparation, usually by formal legal process.
senses.example: to recover damages in trespass; to recover debt and costs in a legal action or that is owing

senses.definition: A position of holding a firearm during exercises, whereby the lock is at shoulder height and the sling facing out.
(dated) The forward movement in rowing, after one stroke to take another (recovery).
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To get better after an illness or injury, or return to normal health and strength.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, KUV, with a short u as in 'cup.' The final syllable is an unstressed American r-colored schwa, so it sounds like 'ur,' not 'ver.'

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes returning to health, safety or normal life.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech recover is very common in health contexts: 'She is recovering from surgery' or 'How long does recovery take?' People also say 'get better' or 'bounce back' in casual talk. Recover also means to get back lost property, as in 'The police recovered the stolen car.' The noun recovery is used for health and for data restoration.

distinctions.note: Heal focuses on injuries closing or wounds mending; recover is broader and refers to regaining overall health or strength.
Get better is the everyday, informal phrase; recover sounds more formal and is common in medical and written contexts.
Retrieve means to fetch or bring back something you lost; recover can also mean recovering health or a state of mind.

examples.everyday: My dad is finally recovering from his knee surgery, and he can walk to the mailbox again.
examples.professional: After the outage, we recovered the lost records from our backups within two hours.
examples.analytical: Job's account shows a man who, though stripped of everything, struggles to recover a sense of meaning before God.

nuance.analogy: To recover is like a plant that wilts in a dry week and then stands upright again once it gets water and sunlight.
nuance.etymology: From Latin recuperare, 'to get back,' via Old French recovrer.
common_mistakes: Using recover with 'of' in place of 'from' (recover from an illness, not recover of an illness).
Confusing recover with recovery when you need the noun; say 'her recovery' rather than 'her recover.'

recover.etymology: From Middle English *recoveren*, *rekeveren*, from Anglo-Norman *recoverer* and Old French *recovrer*, from Latin *recupero*, alternative form of *recipero*.

conversation.text: It took me a week to recover from the flu.
He's recovering at home after his knee surgery.
Give your body time to recover after a long run.

senses.definition: (uncommon) A priest or bishop in the Orthodox Church who is in charge of a parish or in an administrative leadership position in a theological seminary or academy.
senses.label: uncommon

senses.definition: In the Anglican Church, a cleric in charge of a parish and who owns the tithes of it.
In the Roman Catholic Church, a cleric with managerial as well as spiritual responsibility for a church or other institution.
In a Protestant church, a pastor in charge of a church with administrative and pastoral leadership combined.
A headmaster or headmistress in various educational institutions, e.g. a university.

core.definition: A priest in charge of a parish or a church institution such as a seminary, college, or university, responsible for its administration and spiritual life.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, REK, and make the final syllable a quick, r-colored 'er'. Keep the 'ct' cluster clear, so it is not pronounced like 'rep-ter'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, as a religious or institutional title; respectful in church settings.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, rector is most common in the Episcopal Church, where it is the title of the priest in charge of a parish, often addressed as 'Father' or 'Mother' or by the title 'Rector'. In Roman Catholic and Orthodox settings, rector usually means the priest who leads a seminary, shrine, or university. Americans would rarely use the word for a university president, where the term is more common in Europe.

distinctions.note: Pastor is the common Protestant term for the leader of a congregation; rector is the title used mainly in Anglican and Episcopal churches.
Priest is the general word for an ordained minister; rector is a specific office held by a priest who is in charge of a parish or institution.
Dean usually means a senior clergyman of a cathedral or an academic leader of a college; rector is the head of a parish or an institution.

examples.everyday: Our rector invited the whole congregation to the potluck after the Sunday service.
examples.professional: The rector asked the vestry to approve the budget for the new youth ministry before the next fiscal year.
examples.analytical: In the Episcopal tradition, the rector holds canonical responsibility for the parish, while the vestry handles many of its financial and property matters.

nuance.analogy: Like the captain of a ship who is responsible for both steering and the crew's well-being.
nuance.etymology: From Latin rector, meaning 'ruler' or 'governor', from regere 'to rule, to guide'.
common_mistakes: Using rector for a university president in American English; the president is the usual title there.
Mispronouncing it as 'rec-TOR' with stress on the second syllable.

traditions.view: In Orthodox churches a rector is usually a priest or bishop who heads a theological school or seminary, or who serves a parish, depending on local custom.

A rector is a priest appointed to direct a church, seminary, university or other institution, with managerial as well as spiritual duties; the role is defined by canon law and differs from a pastor of a territorial parish.

Anglican and Episcopal churches use rector for the priest in charge of a parish, supported by a lay vestry. Lutheran and Reformed churches generally use pastor or minister, so rector is not a standard office for most Protestants.

rector.etymology: Middle English *rectour*, *rector*, from Old French *rector*, *rectour* and Latin *rēctor*.

senses.definition: An equation that recursively defines a sequence; each term of the sequence is defined as a function of the preceding terms.

core.definition: A mathematical equation that defines each term of a sequence using one or more of the preceding terms.

pronunciation.tip: Stress recurrence on KUR and relation on LAY, which keeps a lighter secondary stress. The first syllable of relation is reduced, so say rih-LAY-shun, not REL-ay-shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: This phrase appears in math, computer science and data science courses and textbooks, rarely outside those fields. In lectures Americans often say the full phrase, but in fast technical talk they may shorten it to recurrence. In a meeting, say recurrence and listeners will usually understand from context. Avoid it in casual conversation unless the topic is math.

distinctions.note: Recursion is the process of a definition or function calling itself, while a recurrence relation is a specific equation that uses this idea to define a sequence.
A closed-form solution gives any term directly from its position, while a recurrence relation builds each term from earlier ones.
Difference equation is a close synonym used especially when studying discrete change, and the two are often treated as the same thing.

collocations: initial conditions of a recurrence relation

examples.everyday: My kid's math homework asked us to write a recurrence relation, and I had to look it up.
examples.professional: We can model customer retention with a recurrence relation that updates each month from the previous month's value.
examples.analytical: A recurrence relation defines the sequence through its initial terms and a rule for generating later ones, so proofs about it often use induction.

nuance.analogy: Like a recipe that says to get the next step, take the last result and add two, a recurrence relation builds each term from earlier ones.
nuance.etymology: Recurrence comes from Latin recurrere, to run back; relation comes from Latin relatio, a carrying back.
common_mistakes: Saying recurrent relation; the standard term is recurrence relation.
Confusing a recurrence relation with a closed-form formula, which computes any term without the earlier ones.
Stressing the first syllable of relation as REL-ation instead of rih-LAY-shun.

core.definition: A Persian-era name in Ezra and Nehemiah, borne by several men, most notably a royal official who opposed rebuilding Jerusalem.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the final syllable short and reduced, like the 'um' in 'hum'. Avoid adding a second stressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a proper name, so it carries no evaluative sense, though in Ezra 4 the man bearing it plays an obstructive role.
nuance.usage_note: Rehum appears only in biblical and historical discussion, so Americans would use it in Bible study, sermons, or church history talk. It is not a common given name today. When mentioning him, you can say 'Rehum, the official in Ezra 4' to make the reference clear.

examples.everyday: At our Bible study, someone asked who Rehum was, and we spent ten minutes on Ezra 4.
examples.professional: In my commentary on Ezra, Rehum is the regional official whose letter helped stop the rebuilding.
examples.analytical: Ezra 4 presents Rehum as a provincial official whose letter to Artaxerxes shows how local politics shaped the restoration.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew rehum, traditionally glossed as 'merciful' or 'compassionate'; the derivation is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing Rehum with Rehoboam, a different son of Solomon.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew name is Rechum (רְחוּם), a personal name of uncertain meaning. Ezra 2:2 lists Rehum among the leaders who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. Ezra 4:8-23 describes Rehum the commander, who with Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes accusing the Jews of rebuilding Jerusalem as a rebellious city, which led to the work being halted. Nehemiah 3:17 names Rehum the son of Bani as repairing a section of the wall, showing a different man of the same name working on the rebuilding.

senses.definition: To fall back again; to slide or turn back into a former state or practice.
senses.example: He has improved recently but keeps relapsing into states of utter confusion.

senses.definition: To return to a vice, especially self-harm or alcoholism, failing to maintain abstinence.
senses.example: relapsed after 5 months of being clean

senses.definition: To slip or slide back physically; to turn back.
To recur; to worsen, be aggravated (after a period of improvement).
The act or situation of relapsing.
senses.example: a drug relapse

senses.definition: An occasion when a person becomes ill again after a period of improvement.

core.definition: To return to a previous bad state, such as an illness, a habit or a problem, after a period of improvement.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, -LAPS, and the final s is a clear s sound. The first syllable is short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a setback, especially in health, recovery or addiction, and it carries a sense of disappointment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use relapse most often for health, especially addiction, illness or recovery programs, as in 'He relapsed after six months of sobriety.' In everyday conversation people might also say 'slip back' or 'fall back into bad habits.' A sympathetic response is 'That's tough, but you can try again.'

distinctions.note: Recur means to happen again in general, often without a sense of return to an earlier state, while relapse usually describes returning to a bad condition after recovering.
Regress is more formal and describes going backward in development or progress, while relapse is most often used for illness or habits.

examples.everyday: My uncle was doing great after the surgery, but he had a relapse last week and is back in the hospital.
examples.professional: The clinic tracks the relapse rate for each treatment program to evaluate outcomes.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's account of akrasia treats the agent who relapses into vice as one who knows the good but fails to act on that knowledge.

nuance.analogy: A relapse is like a boat that drifts back toward the shore it just left after the rowers stopped pulling.
nuance.etymology: From Latin relabi (to slide back), from re- (back) and labi (to slip).
common_mistakes: Using relapse with a preposition incorrectly; say 'relapse into' a habit or 'relapse to' a condition.
Confusing the verb and noun pronunciation; in American English both are stressed on the second syllable.

relapse.etymology: From Latin *relapsus*, past participle of *relabi* (“to slide back, fall back”), from *re-* (“back”) + *labi* (“to slip, slide, fall”).

senses.definition: A storage location for files, such as downloadable software packages, or files in a source control system.
A location for storage, often for safety or preservation.
A burial vault.
A person to whom a secret is entrusted.
(dated) A place where things are stored for sale; a shop.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A place where things are stored, often in an organized way, such as a collection of files or a storage location for valuable items.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PAH. Use the American cot vowel, which is a low AH sound, and make the r in "tor" clear. The final syllable is a light "-ee."

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a place of storage, and can be positive if the place holds something valuable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "repository" in professional and technical settings, especially in software engineering, where it means a place where code is stored. In everyday speech it appears for archives, libraries, or collections, and sounds a bit formal. For casual storage, people say "storage" or "collection."

distinctions.note: "Archive" usually refers to historical records kept for long-term preservation. "Repository" can be any storage place, including active code systems.
"Storage" is everyday and general. "Repository" sounds more formal and suggests an organized collection.

examples.everyday: The local library is a repository of old newspapers and family histories for the whole county.
examples.professional: Please push your changes to the shared code repository before the release on Friday.
examples.analytical: Scripture functions as a repository of the church's memory, preserving the narratives on which its faith rests.

nuance.analogy: A repository is like a well-organized filing cabinet where every document has a labeled drawer.
nuance.etymology: From Latin repositorium, "a storeroom," from reponere, "to put back, store."
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle syllables; the -ory ending is "-or-ee," not "-ory" with a long o.
Using "repository" for a casual storage closet; it sounds formal in everyday speech.

senses.definition: To cancel or postpone the punishment of someone, especially an execution.
To bring relief to someone.
To abandon or postpone plans to close, withdraw or abolish (something).
The cancellation or postponement of a punishment.
senses.example: The prisoner was saved from execution; the governor had requested a reprieve.

senses.definition: A document authorizing such an action.
Relief from pain etc. especially temporary.
A cancellation or postponement of a proposed event undesired by many.

core.definition: To cancel or postpone someone's punishment, especially an execution, or to give someone temporary relief from a problem.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, which ends in a long ee sound, so the word is rih-PREEV, not 'REP-reeve'. The first syllable is quick and weak.

nuance.connotation: Positive for the person receiving relief, though the word often appears in serious legal or emotional contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reprieve mainly for legal delays, such as a governor's reprieve of an execution, and for welcome breaks from trouble, as in 'a brief reprieve from the heat'. Casual speakers may say 'a break' or 'a breather'. The noun form is common in news reports.

distinctions.note: A pardon forgives the offense and removes guilt; a reprieve only delays or cancels punishment for now.
A stay is a court order that temporarily stops an action; reprieve is broader and can describe a governor's delay.

examples.everyday: The rain held off all afternoon, which gave us a welcome reprieve from the heat.
examples.professional: Finance agreed to a reprieve on the budget cuts until we see the third-quarter numbers.
examples.analytical: Mercy in criminal law is often framed as a reprieve that defers judgment rather than a full pardon that cancels the offense.

nuance.analogy: Like pressing pause on a verdict: the outcome stays the same, but the clock stops for now.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French reprive, from reprendre 'to take back'.
common_mistakes: Using reprieve for a permanent escape; a reprieve is usually temporary.
Stressing the first syllable as REP-reeve instead of rih-PREEV.

senses.definition: To reject the truth or validity of; to deny.
To refuse to have any relation to; to disown.
To refuse to pay or honor (a debt).
To be repudiated. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
Repudiated by a husband, divorced.
Repudiated after betrothal or engagement.
Set aside, rejected.
A divorced wife.

core.definition: To formally reject or deny a belief, claim, or relationship, often publicly, and to disown or refuse to accept it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'PYOO', and the last syllable is a clear 'ayt'. Do not stress the final syllable as in 'ray-DATE'.

nuance.connotation: Negative to serious. It implies a strong, deliberate rejection, often with consequences.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'repudiate' in news, politics, legal writing, and formal statements, such as 'The senator repudiated the remarks.' In everyday talk, 'disown', 'reject', or 'distance myself from' is more natural. The word sounds stiff or dramatic in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Reject is common and neutral, used for ideas, offers, or people. Repudiate is more formal and emphasizes a public, deliberate disavowal.
Deny usually means saying something is not true. Repudiate often means rejecting a belief, claim, or association, not just its truth.

examples.everyday: My brother repudiated the rumor about him right away on social media.
examples.professional: The company repudiated the vendor's claims after the audit found no evidence of the defect.
examples.analytical: The author repudiates the earlier thesis, arguing that its foundational premise cannot survive contemporary evidence.

nuance.analogy: To repudiate a claim is like tearing a signed contract in front of witnesses: you are publicly refusing to be bound by it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin repudiare, 'to reject, divorce', from repudium, 'divorce, rejection'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in 'ri-PEW-di-AYT'.
Using 'repudiate' to mean 'repeat', which is a different verb.

repudiate.etymology: from Latin *repudiātus*, the perfect passive participle of *repudiō* (“to cast off, reject”) (see *-ate*), from *repudium* (“rejection, repudiation, divorce”).

senses.definition: Offensive or repulsive; arousing disgust or aversion.
Opposed or in conflict.
senses.example: a repugnant condition

core.definition: Extremely unpleasant or morally offensive, causing strong disgust or rejection.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the 'PUG' syllable and keep the hard 'g'. The final 'ant' is a weak 'unt', not 'ant' like the insect.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes something morally or physically offensive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'repugnant' in formal debate, editorials, and writing about moral issues, as in 'a repugnant idea.' In casual talk, 'gross', 'disgusting', or 'totally unacceptable' is more natural. It is a strong word, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Offensive is common and can mean rude or insulting. Repugnant is stronger and suggests a deep moral or physical disgust.
Unpleasant is mild and everyday. Repugnant is much stronger and sounds formal.

examples.everyday: I find the way they talk about their neighbors completely repugnant.
examples.professional: The proposal to hide the failed test results is repugnant to our safety standards.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers argue that a conclusion which is repugnant to moral intuition should cast doubt on the premises that produced it.

nuance.analogy: Something repugnant is like a bad smell that clings to your clothes: you want to get it off immediately.
nuance.etymology: From Latin repugnans, present participle of repugnare, 'to fight against'.
common_mistakes: Using it for mild dislike, which overstates the feeling.
Pronouncing it with a silent 'g' as in 'rih-PUN-ant'.

repugnant.etymology: From Middle English *repugnaunt*, from Old French *repugnant*, borrowed from Latin *repugnans*, present participle of *repugnare* (“to oppose, to fight against”), from *re-* (“back, against”) + *pugnare* (“to fight”); see *pugnacious*.

senses.definition: Tending to rouse aversion or to repulse; disgusting.
senses.example: a repulsive smell

senses.definition: Cold; reserved; forbidding.
Having the capacity to repel.

core.definition: Extremely unpleasant and causing disgust, or able to push things away, as in physics.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable. The final 'ive' is a short 'iv' sound, not 'eve'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes something that disgusts people, such as food, behavior or a person's manner.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'repulsive' often in everyday speech to describe disgusting things or behavior. It is a strong word, so use it with care; 'gross' is more casual, and 'really unpleasant' is softer. In formal writing it can also describe a person's cold or forbidding manner.

distinctions.note: 'Disgusting' is the everyday word; 'repulsive' is slightly more formal and can describe moral as well as physical disgust.
'Unattractive' means not pleasing to look at; 'repulsive' means strongly disgusting or revolting.

examples.everyday: That gas station bathroom was absolutely repulsive, so I just waited until we got home.
examples.professional: The vendor's response to our complaint was repulsive, and we are terminating the contract.
examples.analytical: Hume thought that cruelty is repulsive to human nature, and that this repulsion is a basic moral sentiment.

nuance.analogy: Like a bad smell that makes you step back, a repulsive thing pushes you away.
nuance.etymology: From Latin repulsivus, from repellere 'to drive back'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (REP-ul-sive); the stress is on the second syllable.
Using 'repulsive' for mild dislike; it is a strong word, so 'not my favorite' is better in polite talk.

repulsive.etymology: Middle French *repulsif*, from Medieval Latin *repulsivus*, from Latin *repulsus*.

senses.definition: Compensation for damage or loss; amends.
Retaliation or reprisal; vengeance.
Return in kind; recompense, repayment, reward.

core.definition: Payback or reward given in return for something, such as a kindness, a wrong or a service.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'KWY'. The final 'al' is a reduced 'ul' sound, not 'al' as in 'pal'.

nuance.connotation: Can be positive (a fair reward) or negative (revenge), depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'requital' in everyday speech. It appears mainly in formal writing, literature or religious contexts. In conversation, people say 'repayment', 'reward' or 'payback'. The meaning ranges from kind return to revenge, so context matters.

distinctions.note: 'Repayment' usually refers to returning borrowed money; 'requital' can mean any return in kind, including favors or revenge.
'Revenge' always means harm in return for harm; 'requital' can be neutral or positive.

examples.everyday: My brother drove me to the airport, so I bought him dinner as a small requital.
examples.professional: The company offered a bonus as requital for the team's work on the migration.
examples.analytical: Kant insists that justice is not a personal requital but a principle that holds for everyone.

nuance.analogy: Requital is like returning an echo: whatever is sent out comes back in a matching form.
nuance.etymology: From requite, from Old French and Latin requitare, with the noun suffix '-al'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'requital' with 'requisition' or 'requisite', which look similar but are unrelated.
Using it for a simple thank-you; it suggests a return that balances something given.

senses.definition: Marked or characterized by respect.
senses.example: It is of great importance that you act in a respectful manner towards the duke and duchess.

core.definition: Showing courtesy and high regard for another person's feelings, rights, opinions or abilities.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SPEKT, and the final -ful is a weak syllable, so say it as 'fuhl', not 'full'. The t before -ful is clear, so don't drop it.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone's courtesy and consideration; the opposite of 'disrespectful', which can sound like an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'respectful' often in everyday talk, at work and in schools, to describe how someone behaves toward others. You can say 'Be respectful' to a child or 'She's very respectful of other people's time' in a meeting. Use 'respectful of' with a noun, not 'respectful to' for attitudes.

distinctions.note: 'Respectable' means acceptable or decent in others' eyes; 'respectful' describes how you show regard to someone.
'Polite' is about everyday manners; 'respectful' suggests deeper regard for a person's dignity or authority.

examples.everyday: My son is really respectful to his grandparents when they visit.
examples.professional: Please keep the feedback respectful and focused on the code, not the person who wrote it.
examples.analytical: A respectful reading of the text attends to its author's intent rather than imposing modern categories on it.

nuance.analogy: Like taking off your hat in a church: the act itself shows you recognize something valuable in the place.
nuance.etymology: From Latin respectus, 'a looking back, regard', from respicere 'to look back at'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'respectful to' for an attitude; 'respectful of' is more natural with abstract nouns like rights or privacy.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'full' instead of the weak 'fuhl'.

senses.definition: Part of or similar to rhetoric, the use of language as a means to persuade.
Not earnest, or presented only for the purpose of an argument.
Asked for dramatic or persuasive effect, rather than to get an answer.
senses.example: '"Are you an idiot? Actually, don't answer that, it was rhetorical."

senses.definition: (dated) A study or exercise in rhetoric.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Relating to persuasive language, or used for effect rather than to be taken literally or to get a real answer.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, TOR, and the first and last syllables are reduced. Many Americans pronounce the middle vowel like 'aw' (cot-caught merger), so 'rih-TAR-ih-kul' is also common.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rhetorical mostly in school, writing, and discussion. 'Rhetorical question' is the most common phrase, and in casual conversation people often use it to mean that a question needs no answer, such as 'Well, rhetorical question: who likes taxes?'. Calling a speech 'rhetorical' can suggest it is empty.

distinctions.note: Figurative describes language that uses images or non-literal meaning, while rhetorical describes language used to persuade or create effect.
Literal means exactly what the words say, while rhetorical language may say one thing and mean another for effect.

examples.everyday: When my dad asked who wanted to clean the garage, it was a rhetorical question; he was not asking for volunteers.
examples.professional: Her rhetorical strategy was to open with the customer's complaint and then show how the data supported her proposal.
examples.analytical: Augustine's rhetorical method in the Confessions uses questions addressed to God, so the questions express prayer as much as argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a theater performance: the words are staged to produce an effect on the audience rather than to report facts.
nuance.etymology: From Latin rhetoricus, from Greek rhētorikos, of an orator, from rhētōr, orator.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'rhetorical' with 'rhetoric' as nouns; use the adjective before a noun ('rhetorical device').
Assuming 'rhetorical' means 'false'; it often means used for effect, not necessarily untrue.

rhetorical.etymology: From Middle English *rethorycal*, *rethoricalle*, *rethorycall*, from *rethorik*, *rhetoric* or Latin *rēthoricus*, *rhētoricus*, from Ancient Greek *ῥητορικός* (“concerning public speaking”).

senses.definition: Initialism of reinforcement learning from human feedback, a method for post-training models.

core.definition: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: training a model to prefer responses that people rate as better.

pronunciation.tip: Say each letter separately, as ar, el, aych, and then EF with the main stress on the final letter. Do not say it as one word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical term in machine learning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans in AI and data science say the letters one by one. In meetings, the term appears in discussions of model training and alignment, such as whether an RLHF step improved answers. Outside technical teams, people usually explain it as human feedback training.

distinctions.note: Supervised learning uses labeled examples of correct answers, while RLHF uses human preferences to guide a reward signal.
Fine-tuning is a broad term for further training a model; RLHF is one specific method of fine-tuning using human feedback.

examples.everyday: My friend who works on chatbots says the answers got more helpful after they added RLHF.
examples.professional: We need to finish the RLHF stage before the next release, so the reward model has time to be evaluated.
examples.analytical: RLHF raises questions about whose preferences a model learns, since the feedback comes from a limited group of raters.

nuance.analogy: RLHF is like a coach who watches a player's performance and rewards the moves that people judge to be best.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of reinforcement learning from human feedback.
common_mistakes: Saying RLHF as one word, like rel-hiff.
Using RLHF for any kind of human labeling; it specifically refers to a preference-based reward training process.

conversation.text: Our RLHF pipeline has three stages: supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and policy optimization.
Some sycophancy is often attributed to RLHF, because raters tend to prefer agreeable answers.
We don't have the rater budget for full RLHF, so let's try DPO on the preference data we already have.

senses.definition: A clear, deep, red variety of corundum, valued as a precious stone.
A deep red color.
senses.example: ruby:

senses.definition: The tincture red or gules.
A ruby hummer, a South American hummingbird, Clytolaema rubricauda.
A red bird-of-paradise, Paradisaea rubra.
A pronunciation guide written above or beside Chinese characters.
Of a deep, red color; ruby-red.
(poetic) To make red; to redden.
senses.label: poetic

core.definition: A precious gemstone that is a deep red variety of the mineral corundum, valued as jewelry.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ROO, and make the final vowel a clear, long 'ee'. The 'r' is a full American r, not a trilled or tapped sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests beauty, wealth, and value, and it is used for jewelry, anniversaries, and descriptions of something precious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ruby for the stone, the color, and as a name, as in a ruby anniversary (40th) and ruby-red grapefruit. In casual talk people say 'ruby red' for the color. Used for a person, it sounds affectionate but old-fashioned unless it is a name.

distinctions.note: A garnet is a different mineral that is usually darker and less bright; a ruby is a red corundum.
Red is the general color word; ruby suggests a deep, rich, gem-like red.

examples.everyday: She wore a ruby ring to my cousin's wedding, and everyone asked about it.
examples.professional: The jeweler's report listed the stone as a ruby with no heat treatment noted.
examples.analytical: In Proverbs, the ruby stands for a woman's worth, and the image makes value depend on character rather than possession.

nuance.analogy: Like a drop of wine caught in sunlight, glowing deep red.
nuance.etymology: From Old French rubi, from Medieval Latin rubinus, from Latin rubeus, 'red.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'ruby' with 'rubies' in the plural form or using 'rubys'.
Using 'ruby' for any red stone, when only red corundum is a true ruby.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the Hebrew word peninim is usually translated 'rubies' or 'pearls,' and it refers to costly precious stones. The term is used to show that wisdom and virtue are worth more than any jewel. Proverbs 31:10 compares a capable wife to rubies, saying her worth is far above them. Job 28:18 says wisdom is worth more than pearls or coral, and Lamentations 4:7 describes the princes' bodies as ruddy, comparing them to coral.

senses.definition: A bag; especially a large bag of strong, coarse material for storage and handling of various commodities, such as potatoes, coal, coffee; or, a bag with handles used at a supermarket, a grocery sack; or, a small bag for small items, a satchel.

The amount a sack holds; also, an archaic or historical measure of varying capacity, depending on commodity type and according to local usage; an old English measure of weight, usually of wool, equal to 13 stone (182 pounds), or in other sources, 26 stone (364 pounds).
The plunder and pillaging of a captured town or city.
senses.example: the sack of Rome

senses.definition: Loot or booty obtained by pillage.
A successful tackle of the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage.
Dismissal from employment, or discharge from a position.
senses.example: give (someone) the sack

senses.definition: Bed.
senses.example: hit the sack

senses.definition: The scrotum.
senses.example: He got passed the ball, but it hit him in the sack.

senses.definition: Any disposable bag.
One of the square bases anchored at first base, second base, or third base.
senses.example: He twisted his ankle sliding into the sack at second.

senses.definition: (dated) A kind of loose-fitting gown or dress with sleeves which hangs from the shoulders, such as a gown with a Watteau back or sack-back, fashionable in the late 17th to 18th century; or, formerly, a loose-fitting hip-length jacket, cloak or cape.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) A sack coat; a kind of coat worn by men, and extending from top to bottom without a cross seam.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) A variety of light-colored dry wine from Spain or the Canary Islands; also, any strong white wine from southern Europe; sherry.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To put in a sack or sacks.
senses.example: Help me sack the groceries.

senses.definition: To bear or carry in a sack upon the back or the shoulders.
To plunder or pillage, especially after capture; to obtain spoils of war from.
senses.example: The barbarians sacked Rome in 410 CE.

senses.definition: To tackle the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage, especially before he is able to throw a pass.
To discharge from a job or position; to fire.
senses.example: He was sacked last September.

senses.definition: To give up on, to abandon, delay, to not think about someone or something.
senses.example: Sack the homework.

core.definition: A large bag of coarse material used for storing or carrying goods such as potatoes, flour, or coal.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short a in cat, and end with a clear k sound. Do not add an extra vowel after the k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word is descriptive and not usually emotional.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say bag for a grocery bag, but sack is still common for a large bag of potatoes, flour, or grain, and in the phrase sack lunch. Sack is also used in football for tackling a quarterback. To fire someone, Americans say fired rather than get the sack, which is more British.

distinctions.note: Bag is the general everyday word, while sack suggests a larger, rougher bag used for bulk goods.
A pack is a bundle carried on the back, while a sack is a bag for storing or carrying bulk material.

examples.everyday: Can you grab that sack of potatoes from the trunk before we go inside?
examples.professional: The warehouse receives every shipment of grain in fifty-pound sacks, so we track the weight at intake.
examples.analytical: The biblical sack was a simple container of coarse cloth, and its ordinariness made it a powerful image of provision.

nuance.analogy: Like a loose canvas bag for bulk goods, rough and practical.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sacc, from Latin saccus, from Greek sakkos, sackcloth.
common_mistakes: Using sack for a small paper grocery bag, which is more often called a bag.
Saying the word with a long a as in sake instead of the short a in sack.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew saq (sack, coarse cloth). Genesis 37:34 describes Jacob putting on sackcloth to mourn Joseph. Genesis 42:25 says Joseph ordered his brothers' sacks filled with grain, showing the sack as a container for provisions.

sack.etymology: From Middle English *sak*, *sek*, *sach*, *zech* (“bag, sackcloth”), from Old English *sacc* (“sack, bag”) and *sæċċ* (“sackcloth, sacking”); both from **sakku*, from late Proto-Germanic **sakkuz* (“sack”), borrowed from Latin *saccus* (“large bag”), from…

senses.definition: A sacred act and the attendant ceremony, considered an outward sign of divine grace, instituted by Jesus Christ.
The Eucharist.
The consecrated Eucharist (especially the bread).
Anything regarded as possessing a sacred character or mysterious significance.
The oath of allegiance taken by soldiers in Ancient Rome; hence, any sacred ceremony used to impress an obligation; a solemn oath-taking; an oath.
To bind by an oath.

core.definition: A sacred Christian rite that is an outward sign of God's grace, such as baptism or the Eucharist (Lord's Supper).

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SAK. The second syllable is a reduced vowel, so say SAK-ruh-munt, not sak-ra-MENT.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in religious settings; it names something solemn and sacred.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sacrament mainly in church, theology and religious conversation. In Catholic and Orthodox settings it is common, while many Protestant Americans prefer the word ordinance for baptism and the Lord's Supper. The verb meaning to bind by oath is archaic and rare today.

distinctions.note: Ordinance is the preferred Protestant term, especially Baptist, for baptism and the Lord's Supper, while sacrament is common in Catholic and Orthodox usage.
Ritual is any fixed ceremony, religious or not, while a sacrament is specifically a Christian rite believed to convey grace.

examples.everyday: My aunt was baptized as an adult, and she says that sacrament meant a lot to her.
examples.professional: Our parish council is scheduling a training session so new volunteers understand how to prepare families for the sacrament of baptism.
examples.analytical: Augustine defines a sacrament as a visible sign of an invisible grace, a formula that shaped Western theology for centuries.

nuance.analogy: A sacrament works like a wedding ring: a visible object that signifies and carries a deeper commitment that cannot be seen.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sacramentum, a sacred thing or a military oath, a translation of Greek mysterion.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as sak-ruh-MENT
Using sacrament for any religious ceremony rather than a rite believed to convey grace
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture does not use the word sacrament; Latin sacramentum translates Greek mysterion, meaning mystery. Matthew 28:19 links baptism with the Trinity, and 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 describes the Lord's Supper.

traditions.view: Orthodox Christians speak of seven mysteries (sacraments), and they regard the Eucharist as the real presence of Christ, received for union with God.
Catholics count seven sacraments, and they teach that the Eucharist is the true body and blood of Christ under the appearance of bread and wine.
Most Protestants recognize two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, and Lutherans, Reformed and Baptists differ on how Christ is present in the Supper.

sacrament.etymology: From Middle English *sacrament*, from Old French *sacrement*, from Ecclesiastical Latin *sacrāmentum* (“sacrament”), from Latin *sacrō* (“hallow, consecrate”), from *sacer* (“sacred, holy”), originally sum deposited by parties to a suit.

senses.definition: Beyond alteration, criticism, or interference, especially due to religious sanction; inviolable.
Sacred, very holy.

core.definition: Too sacred or important to be changed, questioned, or interfered with, often because of tradition or religious authority.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllable is pronounced with the 'ng' sound followed by a hard k, so do not add a vowel before the final t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly ironic. It can be respectful about true sacred things, but Americans often use it humorously about a habit or policy people refuse to change.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in news, politics, and writing about institutions, for example 'Social Security is treated as sacrosanct.' In casual talk it is more often used jokingly, as in 'My Friday lunch is sacrosanct.' Saying it in everyday conversation can sound a bit stiff, so it works best in writing or serious discussion.

distinctions.note: Sacred describes something holy or set apart for God. Sacrosanct describes something protected from change or criticism, and it can be used for secular things.
Inviolable is a close synonym but more legal and formal. Sacrosanct adds a stronger sense of religious or traditional reverence.

examples.everyday: My Sunday morning run is sacrosanct, so please don't schedule anything before noon.
examples.professional: Our team treats the code review process as sacrosanct, so no change ships without at least one approval.
examples.analytical: For many believers, the canon of Scripture is considered sacrosanct, and any proposal to revise it provokes deep theological resistance.

nuance.analogy: Like a wall built around a sacred garden, a sacrosanct rule is protected so no one can trample it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sacrosanctus, from sacer, sacred, and sanctus, holy.
common_mistakes: Using sacrosanct to mean simply important; it implies that something must not be changed.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: The act of sprinkling salt, as on food or on an icy road.
A salt marsh.
The act of tampering with an investigation site by adding bogus evidence.

core.definition: The act of sprinkling salt on something, especially food or an icy road, to season it or melt ice.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The l is often silent or very faint in American speech, so it sounds like SAW-ting. Do not add an extra vowel between the l and t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a routine practice, such as salting roads in winter or salting food while cooking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use salting mostly as a gerund or noun for the everyday act of adding salt, and in winter news about road crews. The word for the verb is salt, so people say 'They salted the driveway' rather than 'They saltinged it'. In software or security contexts, salting also means adding random data to a password before hashing it, which is a different technical sense.

distinctions.note: Seasoning is the broader act of adding any flavoring, while salting is specifically adding salt.
Salinization is a technical term for the buildup of salt in soil or water, not the act of adding salt to food.

examples.everyday: The city crew was salting the main road before dawn, so the bus was running late.
examples.professional: Our data pipeline includes a salting step before hashing user passwords, so identical passwords produce different hashes.
examples.analytical: The salting of a hash function adds unpredictable input so that precomputed attacks lose their effectiveness.

nuance.analogy: Like adding a pinch of random noise to a secret so that every copy looks different.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sealt, related to Latin sal, salt.
common_mistakes: Saying 'salting' as a verb with the wrong form, instead of using 'salt' in the present or past tense.
Dropping the t sound at the end, which is weak in fast speech but should still be clear.

senses.definition: A place of safety, refuge, or protection.
senses.example: My car is a sanctuary, where none can disturb me except for people who cut me off.

senses.definition: An area set aside for protection.
senses.example: The bird sanctuary has strict restrictions on visitors so the birds aren't disturbed.

senses.definition: A state of being protected, asylum.
senses.example: The government granted sanctuary to the defector, protecting him from his former government.

senses.definition: The consecrated (or sacred) area of a church or temple around its tabernacle or altar.

core.definition: A place of safety or refuge, especially a holy place, or a protected area where people or animals are kept from harm.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the 'ch' sound in the middle; the final syllable is a reduced 'ree' with an American r. Don't split the 'ct' into a 't' plus 'sh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests safety, protection and peace, and it can carry strong moral or political meanings in debates about immigration or asylum.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sanctuary' for a church, a wildlife refuge, or a place where someone is protected, such as a 'sanctuary city' that limits cooperation with immigration enforcement. In a church, the 'sanctuary' is the main worship space, so asking where the sanctuary is means where the services happen. The word can be politically loaded when used for immigration policy.

distinctions.note: A refuge is a shelter from danger or trouble, and it can be informal; a sanctuary is more formal and often an officially protected place or a holy space.
A haven is a safe, comfortable place from stress; a sanctuary can be a formal, legally protected or religious space.

examples.everyday: After the long flight, the quiet garden felt like a sanctuary.
examples.professional: The city council voted to make the building a sanctuary for staff who need a quiet room during high-stress projects.
examples.analytical: In the Hebrew Bible the sanctuary is the place where God uniquely dwells among the people, so its holiness shapes all of Israel's worship.

nuance.analogy: A sanctuary is like a lifeboat in a storm: it is designed to keep you safe while the waves keep crashing outside.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sanctuarium, 'holy place', from sanctus, 'holy'.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle 'ct' as 'k-t' or 'shoo' with extra stress; it is a 'chuh' sound with the stress on the first syllable.
Using 'sanctuary' for any hiding place; in the US it implies official protection or a special holy or wildlife space.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word miqdash means a holy place, a sanctuary, and the Greek hagion refers to the holy place or the sanctuary of God. Exodus 25:8 records God's command to build a sanctuary so that he may dwell among his people. Psalm 73:17 describes the psalmist finding understanding when he went into the sanctuary of God. Hebrews 8:2 presents Christ as minister in the true sanctuary, the heavenly tent that the Lord pitched.

sanctuary.etymology: From Middle English *seyntuarie*, from Old French *saintuaire*, from Late Latin *sanctuarium* (“a sacred place, a shrine, a private cabinet, in Medieval Latin also temple, church, churchyard, cemetery, right of asylum”), from Latin *sanctus* (“holy,…

senses.definition: (of an idea or theory) To prove itself false by showing that falsehood is a logical consequence of the act or situation of holding it to be true.

core.definition: Describing an idea or claim that proves itself false, because its truth would logically require its own falsehood.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable of 'refuting' (fyoo), with 'self' carrying weaker stress. Keep the 't' in 'refuting' soft, closer to a flap between vowels, and don't stress the 'ing'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical judgment about an argument's logic and does not criticize the person making it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this mainly in philosophy, logic, debate and academic writing. Dictionaries list it as a verb, but in practice it works as an adjective describing a claim, such as 'the claim is self-refuting.' In casual talk, people say something like 'that argument defeats itself' instead.

distinctions.note: Contradictory means two statements cannot both be true; self-refuting means one statement, by being asserted, makes itself false.
Invalid describes an argument whose conclusion does not follow; self-refuting describes a claim that undermines itself when held.

examples.everyday: If you say you never believe anything anyone tells you, that's kind of self-refuting, since you just told me something.
examples.professional: Your design doc says all user input is untrusted, then assumes the client always sends valid tokens, which makes the validation rule self-refuting.
examples.analytical: The skeptic's claim that no knowledge is possible is self-refuting, because asserting it presupposes that at least one known truth exists.

nuance.analogy: Like a sign that reads 'This sign is lying': the message destroys its own credibility the moment you believe it.
nuance.etymology: From 'self' (Old English) and 'refute' (from Latin refutare, 'to drive back, repel').
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'self-REF-yoo-ting' with stress on the first syllable of 'refuting'.
Using it as a synonym for 'self-contradictory' in everyday speech, where 'contradicts itself' is more natural.

senses.definition: The ordinal form of the number seventy-two, describing a person or thing in position number 72 of a sequence.
senses.example: The answer appears on the seventy-second page of the book.

senses.definition: Lasting seventy seconds.
One of seventy-two equal parts of a whole.
senses.example: A seventy-second of 1440 is 20.

core.definition: Coming in position number seventy-two in a sequence; also, lasting seventy seconds.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second word, SEC-ond, while the first word gets a weaker stress. Say SEV-en-tee with a short, reduced final syllable, and don't pronounce the d in second as a separate sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a plain counting or ordering term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for ordinal position, such as the seventy-second floor or the seventy-second birthday, and for seventy-second intervals in timing. In ordinary speech people often say the seventy-second one or the 72nd, especially in writing. For dates and numbered items in print, the numeral form 72nd is common.

distinctions.note: Seventy-second is the ordinal (position), while seventy-two is the cardinal (quantity).
Second alone is the ordinal for two; seventy-second is used only for the number 72 in position.

examples.everyday: My grandmother just celebrated her seventy-second birthday with the whole family.
examples.professional: The seventy-second release on our tracker is the one that finally fixed the login bug.
examples.analytical: The seventy-second verse of the chapter shifts the argument from creation to covenant.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner finishing a race in exactly that place: the seventy-second runner crosses after seventy-first and before seventy-third.
nuance.etymology: Formed from seventy plus second, ultimately from Old English seofontig and second (from Latin secundus, following).
common_mistakes: Saying the stress on seventy instead of second in the compound.
Confusing the ordinal seventy-second with the cardinal seventy-two in writing.
nuance.biblical_note: The ordinal form has no distinctive role in Scripture. The cardinal number seventy appears in Luke 10:1 in the RSV, where the Lord appoints seventy others and sends them ahead of him in pairs.

senses.definition: Darkness where light, particularly sunlight, is blocked.
senses.example: The old oak tree gave shade in the heat of the day.

senses.definition: Something that blocks light, particularly in a window.
senses.example: Close the shade, please: it's too bright in here.

senses.definition: A variety of a color, in particular one obtained by adding black (compare tint).
senses.example: I've painted my room in five lovely shades of pink and chartreuse.

senses.definition: A subtle variation in a concept.
senses.example: shades of meaning

senses.definition: An aspect that is reminiscent of something.
senses.example: shades of Groucho Marx

senses.definition: A very small degree of a quantity, or variety of meaning.
senses.example: That is a shade too close.

senses.definition: A ghost or specter; a spirit.
senses.example: Too long have I been haunted by that shade.

senses.definition: A postage stamp showing an obvious difference in color/color to the original printing and needing a separate catalog/catalog entry.
Subtle insults.
senses.example: throw shade

senses.definition: A cover around or above a light bulb, a lampshade.
(historical) A candle-shade.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To shield (someone or something) from light.
senses.example: The old oak tree shaded the lawn in the heat of the day.

senses.definition: To alter slightly.
senses.example: You'll need to shade your shot slightly to the left.

senses.definition: To vary or approach something slightly, particularly in color.
senses.example: The hillside was bright green, shading towards gold in the drier areas.

senses.definition: To darken, particularly in drawing.
senses.example: I draw contours first, gradually shading in midtones and shadows.

senses.definition: To win by a narrow margin.
senses.example: Both parties claimed afterwards that their man did best in the debate, but an early opinion poll suggested Mr Cameron shaded it.

senses.definition: To reduce (a window) so that only its title bar is visible.
To throw shade, to subtly insult someone.
To move slightly from one's normal fielding position.
senses.example: Jones will shade a little to the right on this pitch count.

senses.definition: (rare) To shield oneself from light.
senses.example: We shaded under a huge oak tree.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: An area of darkness where sunlight is blocked, such as the cooler space under a tree or an awning.

pronunciation.tip: Say one syllable with a long a and a clear final d, without adding a vowel after it. Non-native speakers often add a schwa, producing 'shay-id'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Shade is pleasant on a hot day, but it can also suggest something hidden or partly dark.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Let's sit in the shade' or 'It's cooler in the shade' all the time, especially in summer, at parks, barbecues and outdoor restaurants. A window shade in American English is usually a roll-up cover, while a lampshade is the cover on a lamp. The verb is used less often in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: A shadow is a dark shape cast by an object that blocks light, while shade is the sheltered area itself, often where you sit to escape the sun.
Shelter is a covered place that protects you from weather or danger, while shade only protects you from direct sunlight.

collocations: under the shade of a tree

examples.everyday: It's ninety degrees out, so let's grab a table in the shade.
examples.professional: Can we move the outdoor meeting under the shade of the awning? The screen glare is making it hard to read the slides.
examples.analytical: The poem uses shade as a metaphor for mourning, a space where the speaker can retreat from the harsh light of public life.

nuance.analogy: Shade is like a cool pocket of air in a hot room: you step into it to get relief from the heat.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sceadu, meaning shadow or shelter.
common_mistakes: Saying 'shade' for a shadow cast by a person or object, when 'shadow' is more natural for the dark outline itself.
Pronouncing it with two syllables, as 'shay-ed'.

conversation.text: It's way too hot; let's sit in the shade for a bit.
Is there any shade at the picnic area?
The dog is lying in the shade under the table.

core.definition: A son of the Assyrian king Sennacherib who helped murder his father, and in Zechariah a man sent from Bethel to ask the priests about fasting.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, with a clear American r. The final syllable is a reduced "er", so do not stress it as "ZAIR".

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical name with no everyday emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this name outside Bible study, sermons or scholarly discussion of the Old Testament. In a church or Bible class, you might hear it read aloud, and people will pronounce it with stress on the middle syllable. Most listeners will not know the name without context.

distinctions.note: Sharezar is an alternative spelling used in some other English translations, while the RSV uses Sharezer.

examples.everyday: At Bible study we read about Sharezer, one of the sons who killed their father, and everyone found the story shocking.
examples.professional: When teaching the minor prophets, I point out that the name Sharezer appears in Zechariah as a delegation from Bethel.
examples.analytical: The identification of the Sharezer of Zechariah 7:2 with the Assyrian prince of 2 Kings 19:37 is disputed, and scholars weigh it against the different textual traditions of the name.

nuance.analogy: Like a historical footnote whose name you recognize only from a family genealogy.
nuance.etymology: From the Akkadian Šar-ṣa-uṣur, meaning "O god, protect the king".
common_mistakes: Confusing Sharezer with Sharon, which is a place on the coast.
Writing "Sharezar" when quoting the RSV, which uses Sharezer.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the name is Śarʾeṣer, probably from Akkadian meaning "protect the king". 2 Kings 19:37 and Isaiah 37:38 describe Sharezer and his brother Adrammelech murdering their father Sennacherib in the temple of Nisroch and fleeing to Armenia. Zechariah 7:2 names Sharezer and Regem-melech as men sent from Bethel to ask the priests and prophets whether to continue mourning and fasting.

core.definition: A Levite or priest in the post-exilic community of Judah who helped lead worship and sealed the covenant renewal under Ezra and Nehemiah.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the -NYE- syllable, and the final -ah is a light, reduced vowel. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or pronounce the final vowel too strongly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Used almost only in Bible study, sermons and church discussion. Americans reading Nehemiah or 1 Chronicles would say the name as written, usually with the stress on the third syllable.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group got stuck on a list of names, and Shebaniah was one of them.
examples.professional: In the lesson plan, I flagged Shebaniah as a Levite in Nehemiah's covenant list so the students would not confuse him with the other Shebaniahs.
examples.analytical: Shebaniah's appearance among the signatories in Nehemiah 10 shows how the Levitical families took part in the community's public commitment to the law.

nuance.analogy: Like a name on a signed document: his presence confirms who took responsibility for the agreement.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Shebanyahu, meaning 'Yahweh has brought near' or 'Yahweh has grown' (uncertain).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (SHEB-uh-NYE-uh) instead of the middle one.
Confusing him with Shebna, a different royal official in Isaiah and 2 Kings.
nuance.biblical_note: Shebaniah appears in 1 Chronicles 15:24, where he is among the priests who blew trumpets before the ark when David brought it to Jerusalem, and in Nehemiah 10, where he is among the priests and Levites who sealed the covenant to keep the law of God. These passages show him as a worship leader who helped restore the proper religious life of the nation.

senses.definition: Lazy, unmotivated.
Untrustworthy as a result of being incompetent at the job.
Destitute of shifts or expedients; lacking proper means.

core.definition: Lazy and unwilling to work, or lacking the initiative and resourcefulness to make things happen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SHIFT. The final -less is a short, unstressed 'lis', not 'less' with a long e.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it is a strong criticism of someone's character and effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shiftless mostly in older, folksy, or Southern speech, and in some literary writing. It is a harsh, judgmental word, so using it about a coworker or relative can cause offense. A more neutral alternative is 'not motivated' or 'unproductive'.

distinctions.note: Lazy describes not wanting to work in general; shiftless adds the sense of lacking resourcefulness and getting nothing done.
Shifty means dishonest or evasive, while shiftless means lazy or unproductive, so the two are often confused but mean different things.

examples.everyday: My grandmother called him shiftless, but he just needed a better job.
examples.professional: I can't keep a team member who is shiftless and misses every deadline without telling anyone.
examples.analytical: Critics who call the unemployed shiftless often ignore structural barriers, turning an economic problem into a personal failing.

nuance.analogy: Like a boat with no oars or sail, drifting wherever the current takes it because nobody is steering.
nuance.etymology: From shift (in the sense of resourcefulness or expedient) plus -less.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with shifty, which means evasive or dishonest.
Using it as a mild word; it is a strong insult in American speech.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to or resembling a sibyl or female oracle, especially the Cumaean Sibyl and the Sibylline Books.
Having oracle-like predicting powers, clairvoyant.
Occult, mysterious.
Excessively and exorbitantly expensive. (In allusion to the Sibyl who sold three books to Tarquinius Superbus at the price of the original nine.)
One of the Sibylline Oracles or Sibylline Books.

core.definition: Mysteriously prophetic, like an ancient oracle whose cryptic predictions are hard to interpret.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle vowel to a schwa. The final syllable rhymes with 'line,' not 'lean.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Sibylline is used in literary, classical, and academic writing about prophecy and ancient oracles. Americans would seldom use it in everyday talk. It is most often used to describe cryptic, mysterious statements or a person who seems to speak in riddles.

distinctions.note: Prophetic is the general word for predicting the future, while sibylline emphasizes a cryptic, mysterious, oracle-like manner.
Cryptic describes any puzzling statement, while sibylline specifically suggests an oracle's ambiguous prophecy.

examples.everyday: My grandmother gave us one of her sibylline answers about the weather, and we spent an hour trying to decode it.
examples.professional: The consultant's sibylline comments about the market trend left the team unsure what she actually recommended.
examples.analytical: Her sibylline style of prophecy, which withholds its meaning until events confirm it, complicates the reader's search for a single interpretation.

nuance.analogy: A sibylline statement is like a fortune cookie written by an ancient oracle: it sounds meaningful, but you only understand it afterward.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Sibyllinus, relating to the Sibyl, an ancient prophetess.
common_mistakes: Using 'sibylline' for simple prediction; it implies mystery and ambiguity.
Confusing it with 'sybarite,' which means a person devoted to luxury.

senses.definition: The quality or state of being sincere.

core.definition: The quality of being honest and genuine, so that what you say and feel matches what you mean.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEH, the second syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced vowel, and the t in -ity is often a flapped sound close to 'd' in fast American speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a valued trait of character and communication.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sincerity to describe character and communication, as in 'I appreciated her sincerity' or 'his sincerity came through.' It often appears in discussions of trust and leadership. In casual talk, people more often say 'he means it' or 'she's for real'.

distinctions.note: Honesty means telling the truth; sincerity is the inner genuineness behind what you say, which can be sincere even when mistaken.
Candor is openness and frankness; sincerity focuses on whether the feeling is real.
Integrity is consistent moral principle over time; sincerity is genuineness in a particular expression.

examples.everyday: I could tell from her sincerity that she really meant the apology.
examples.professional: Your feedback was specific, and I appreciated the sincerity behind it.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard insists that faith requires inwardness and sincerity, not merely assent to doctrines.

nuance.analogy: Sincerity is like a clear window: what people show on the outside matches what is actually inside.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sinceritas, from sincerus, meaning pure or unmixed.
common_mistakes: Giving the middle syllable a full vowel like 'seer' instead of a reduced vowel.
Confusing the noun sincerity with the adverb sincerely in a sentence.

sincerity.etymology: From Middle English *sinceritie*, from Old French *sincerité* and Medieval Latin *sincēritās*; both from Latin *sincēritās*, from *sincērus* + *-tās*.

senses.definition: A filthy, slobbering person; a sloven, a villain, a fiend, a louse.
A worthless person.
A drunken or alcoholic person.

core.definition: A dirty, slovenly, worthless person; an old-fashioned insult used mainly for comic effect.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on GUL, the third-from-last syllable area. The middle syllables are weak, so the -er- and -ih- are very reduced; keep the r rhotic but light.

nuance.connotation: Negative and deliberately colorful. It is mostly used playfully or theatrically, and it sounds old-fashioned and mocking.
nuance.usage_note: Almost no American speaker uses this word in ordinary speech. You might meet it in older novels, Shakespeare-era comedy, or as a playful insult among friends. If you use it today, it will sound theatrical, so use a plain word like slob or lowlife instead.

distinctions.note: Slob is a common, informal insult for a messy person, while slubberdegullion is archaic and mostly comic.
Sloven is a slightly more formal word for a person who is untidy or careless about appearance.

examples.everyday: You old slubberdegullion, you left the milk out again.
examples.professional: In the old comedy, the drunken steward is a slubberdegullion who keeps the audience laughing.
examples.analytical: The author's choice of slubberdegullion marks the character as a figure of coarse comedy rather than moral seriousness.

nuance.analogy: It is like a costume word: it looks striking on stage, but no one wears it in daily clothes.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; probably from dialect slubber, meaning to slobber, with an added term of abuse.
common_mistakes: Using it seriously in modern conversation, where it sounds like a joke.
Misspelling it as slubberdegulion, missing the second e and the double letters.

senses.definition: In a solemn manner.

core.definition: In a serious, dignified, or sincere way, often when making a promise or showing deep feeling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is nearly silent, so the word sounds like two beats: SAH-lum and lee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It implies sincerity and gravity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use solemnly when someone makes a serious pledge, a formal promise, or a sad announcement. In casual talk people often say 'seriously' or 'for real' instead. It sounds natural in speeches, letters, and emotional moments.

distinctions.note: Seriously is casual and can mean very much or truly; solemnly stresses dignity and a formal, weighty manner.
Sincerely focuses on honesty of feeling; solemnly focuses on ceremony and gravity of the act.

examples.everyday: My dad solemnly promised he would finally fix the back porch this weekend.
examples.professional: The team leader solemnly committed to meeting the compliance deadline in front of the whole staff.
examples.analytical: The witness solemnly affirmed that the record had not been altered after the hearing.

nuance.etymology: From solemn plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Dropping the middle syllable entirely, which sounds unnatural; keep the light schwa.
Using solemnly for casual promises, which sounds overly dramatic in everyday talk.

senses.definition: A fixed verse form of Italian origin consisting of fourteen lines that are typically five-foot iambics and rhyme according to one of a few prescribed schemes.
To compose sonnets.
To celebrate in sonnets; to write a sonnet about.

core.definition: A fixed poem of fourteen lines, usually in iambic pentameter, with a set rhyme scheme, often used for love poems or serious reflection.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SAH-nit. The second syllable is a reduced 'it', not 'et', and the final t is lightly released rather than a strong 'tuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sonnet in English class, poetry readings and discussions of literature. It is not a casual word, but most educated speakers know it. You can say 'Shakespeare's sonnets' or 'she writes sonnets' naturally in conversation about poetry.

distinctions.note: Poem is the general word for any verse; sonnet names one specific form with fourteen lines and a set rhyme scheme.
An ode is a longer lyric poem of praise with irregular stanzas, while a sonnet is short and follows a strict form.

examples.everyday: My daughter wrote a sonnet about her cat for school, and it was surprisingly good.
examples.professional: For the poetry festival, the committee asked each author to submit one sonnet of exactly fourteen lines.
examples.analytical: Shakespeare's sonnets turn their final couplet into an argument that resolves the tension built in the first twelve lines.

nuance.analogy: A sonnet is like a sealed jar: the form is fixed in size and shape, and the poet must fit the content inside it.
nuance.etymology: From Italian sonetto, a diminutive of suono, 'sound, song'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle 'nn' as a long 'ay' sound or as 'soh-net'.
Using sonnet for any short poem, when the word means one strict form.

sonnet.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *sonnet*, from Italian *sonetto*, from Old Occitan *sonet* (“a song”), diminutive of *son* (“song, sound”), from Latin *sonus* (“sound”).

senses.definition: A female sorcerer, especially one who is elegant; compare witch.

core.definition: A woman who practices magic or sorcery, often with supernatural powers in stories or legend.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SOR, the first syllable. The middle vowel is a reduced uh, and the ending -ess is a short, unstressed ris, not ress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in fiction, negative in moral or religious discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sorceress mainly in fantasy, literature, or historical writing. In everyday talk, people more often say sorcerer without a gender marker, or witch for a folk practitioner. Calling a real woman a sorceress is unusual and can sound like a dated compliment about her charm.

distinctions.note: A witch often suggests folk magic and a sinister figure; sorceress is more elegant and literary.
Sorcerer is the general term for both genders; sorceress specifically marks a woman.

examples.everyday: In the movie, the sorceress turns the villagers into stone with one gesture.
examples.professional: The game's plot is built around a sorceress who controls the weather, so the design team had to match her powers to the story.
examples.analytical: In the Hebrew law of Exodus 22:18, the sorceress is named explicitly, which shows that the ban was framed around the threat of women's magic.

nuance.analogy: A sorceress in a fairy tale is like a queen of an enchanted forest: magnificent, feared, and always at the center of the plot.
nuance.etymology: From sorcerer with the feminine suffix -ess, from Old French sorcier.
common_mistakes: Using sorceress for any female magician; the word fits fantasy and legend better than real stage performers.
Stressing the second syllable, which is the wrong pattern for this word.
nuance.biblical_note: Exodus 22:18 in the RSV says 'You shall not permit a sorceress to live,' using the Hebrew mekashepah, a feminine form of the verb kashaph, to practice magic. The verse belongs to a list of capital offenses in the Covenant Code. Deuteronomy 18:10-11 lists the practitioner of sorcery among forbidden practices, showing that the ban covered all forms of magical manipulation.

senses.definition: (rare) A scarcity of males.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A scarcity of males in a population, or a shortage of men relative to women.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the second syllable, NEER. The final -ia is a light unstressed syllable, not a separate long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a rare, descriptive term from demography and older scholarship.
nuance.usage_note: Spaneria is an obscure word that most American speakers will never hear in conversation. Use it only in historical or demographic writing, and expect many readers to need a definition. In everyday talk, say there are fewer men than women or describe a gender imbalance.

distinctions.note: Gynecocracy refers to government or dominance by women, which is a political concept, while spaneria refers only to a numerical shortage of males.

examples.professional: The demographic report notes a spaneria in the region, which may affect marriage rates and labor patterns.
examples.analytical: Historians have used the term spaneria to describe population imbalances caused by war, emigration or selective mortality.

nuance.analogy: Like a team with too few players of one kind, the population has a shortage of males.
common_mistakes: Confusing spaneria with span or spanner because of the shared letters.
Using it as a common everyday word; most listeners will not know it, so explain it or choose a plainer phrase.

senses.definition: To accelerate (something): to increase its speed, to make it go faster.
senses.example: You shouldn't speed up your car when you go around corners.

senses.definition: To accelerate; to increase speed.
senses.example: The car sped up as it went around the corner.

core.definition: To move, work, or happen faster than before.

pronunciation.tip: As a phrasal verb, the stress usually falls on UP. In speech, the two words link together, so it sounds like 'speed-UP', not two separate words.

nuance.connotation: Neutral or positive. It can be used to request faster progress, but may sound pushy if said to someone who is already working hard.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use speed up for cars, projects, deliveries, and processes: 'Can you speed up the line?' In a restaurant or store, a polite version is 'Could you speed things up a little?' To make a request sound gentler, you can say 'Would it be possible to speed this up?'

distinctions.note: Hurry up is more urgent and can sound rude, while speed up is more neutral and process-focused.
Accelerate is more formal and technical, while speed up is everyday American English.

examples.everyday: Could you speed up the coffee order? I have to catch a train.
examples.professional: We need to speed up the code review so the release doesn't slip.
examples.analytical: The argument suggests that technology speeds up social change without necessarily making it wiser.

nuance.analogy: To speed up is like shifting into a higher gear when the road is clear: the same engine works harder and covers more distance.
common_mistakes: Using speed up with a noun between the words incorrectly, such as speed the up; keep the phrase together or place the object before up.
Saying speed up it when the object is a pronoun; the usual order is speed it up.

conversation.text: Speed up a little; you're holding up traffic.
The guy in front always speeds up when I try to pass.
This new tool will speed up our reporting.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or containing spice.
senses.example: He prepared a spicy casserole.

senses.definition: Of a flavor, provoking a burning sensation due to the presence of capsaicin or a similar chemical.
senses.example: This curry is too spicy for me. I can't eat it.

senses.definition: Of a food, flavor, or odor, tangy, zesty, or pungent.
senses.example: She breathed in the strong, spicy aroma.

senses.definition: Of an expression or behavior, vigorous; colorful; stimulating.
senses.example: He is known for his spicy political commentary.

senses.definition: Scandalous.
Risky; mildly aggressive or dangerous.
senses.example: Look at the little wildcub! That's one spicy ball of fur.

senses.definition: Risqué, sexy, racy; mildly pornographic.
senses.example: I don't want my children to see the spicy images on this web site.

core.definition: Having a strong, hot, or pungent flavor, often from chili peppers or other spices.
